The historic SS United States will be sunk off Florida’s Gulf Coast a day earlier than planned after forecasts of heavy winds forced officials to move up the operation. Okaloosa County announced Monday that the 990-foot ocean liner will be deployed as the world’s largest artificial reef on Wednesday, November 11, instead of Thursday, November 12. Deployment operations are now scheduled to begin at 1 p.m. Central Standard Time. The change comes as the legendary ocean liner makes its final voyage from Mobile, Alabama , to a designated reef site approximately 22 nautical miles southwest of Destin-Fort Walton Beach. “Safety is always a top priority in Okaloosa County,” said County Board Chairman Trey Goodwin. “There is simply no reason to take an unnecessary risk when adjusting the schedule will allow us to carry out this historic deployment safely and smoothly.” The schedule change also means the public sendoff ceremony originally planned for Wednesday afternoon at the Destin-Fort Walton Beach Convention Center has been canceled. However, a public viewing party will still take place at AJ’s Seafood and Oyster Bar in Destin beginning at noon Wednesday. A live feed of the offshore deployment will be shown on the venue’s large outdoor screen, with an online livestream link expected to be posted at thessus.com before operations begin. County officials are also preparing for potentially hundreds of spectator vessels near the deployment site and are urging boaters to follow instructions from safety boats overseeing the operation. The deployment will take place on Veterans Day, adding another layer of significance to the final chapter of America’s most famous ocean liner. Built in 1952, the SS United States still holds the record for the fastest transatlantic crossing by an ocean liner. Following decades of inactivity, the vessel has undergone extensive environmental remediation in Mobile in preparation for its transformation into an artificial reef. The sinking will mark the end of the ship’s 74-year history above water and the beginning of a new role as a diving destination and marine habitat off Florida’s Emerald Coast. articles.title: Marlink Secures BV Certification for XChange NextGen Platform
articles.summary: Marlink has secured Bureau Veritas (BV) type approval for the XChange NextGen edge platform, giving shipowners independent assurance that their onboard digital infrastructure is designed with long-term cyber resilience built-in. For shipowners…
articles.body: Marlink Secures BV Certification for XChange NextGen Platform Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 10, 2026 © Marlink Marlink has secured Bureau Veritas (BV) type approval for the XChange NextGen edge platform, giving shipowners independent assurance that their onboard digital infrastructure is designed with long-term cyber resilience built-in. For shipowners, onboard technology is a long-term investment that can remain in service for years. As software evolves and new services are introduced, cybersecurity must remain a priority throughout the platform’s lifecycle. XChange NextGen’s type approval confirms compliance with requirements covering both cybersecurity capabilities and the processes supporting secure development, maintenance and updates. XChange NextGen is Marlink’s onboard platform, combining edge computing with connectivity, network orchestration, cybersecurity and cloud services to support secure digital operations. Its edge capability allows data to be processed on board, giving shipowners a foundation for analytics and AI applications that depend on reliable data flow between vessel and shore. As part of the Marlink Possibility Portfolio, it reduces hardware complexity and enables vessel and shore teams to deploy, manage and scale digital services more easily across fleets. The certification confirms compliance with IACS UR E27 Rev.1 and Bureau Veritas NR659 requirements within the approved scope. While IACS UR E26 addresses cyber resilience at vessel level, UR E27 focuses on individual onboard systems and equipment, providing shipowners, shipyards and systems integrators with evidence to support applicable class requirements. XChange NextGen’s E27 type approval complements Marlink’s wider approach to vessel cyber resilience. Its OT Security offering helps shipowners identify and manage cyber risks in operational systems, supporting their broader work to meet applicable vessel-level requirements, including IACS UR E26.

articles.title: Boluda Shipping signs agreement for Matrans Terminal in Rotterdam
articles.summary: Boluda Shipping has signed an agreement to acquire Matrans Terminal in Rotterdam, strengthening its planned expansion into Northern Europe. articles.body: Boluda Shipping has signed an agreement to acquire Matrans Terminal in Rotterdam, strengthening its planned expansion into Northern Europe. The agreement was signed on 3 November 2026 and covers the multipurpose terminal in Eemhaven, an important hub for European short-sea shipping. The transaction follows Boluda Shipping’s recent agreement to acquire Samskip . Both acquisitions remain subject to regulatory approvals and other closing conditions. The Matrans deal will give Boluda additional port infrastructure in Rotterdam as it seeks to expand its maritime and intermodal logistics activities. Matrans adds terminal and rail capabilities Matrans Terminal covers approximately 360,000 square metres, including 70,000 square metres of covered warehousing. The facility offers 1,100 metres of quay with a water depth of 12.65 metres. It also includes a Ro-Ro berth with a depth of nine metres and 600 metres of railway track. The terminal handles containers, general cargo, forest products, metals, project cargo and Ro-Ro shipments. In addition, Matrans provides customs services, fiscal representation, road transport and freight forwarding. These activities support cargo movements between the port and inland destinations. Boluda Shipping plans to develop the terminal’s operations, with a focus on improving efficiency, increasing cargo volumes and expanding customer services. However, the company has not disclosed the financial terms of the acquisition. Rotterdam supports Northern European expansion The Matrans agreement forms part of Boluda Shipping’s wider strategy to strengthen its presence in Northern Europe. The company already operates in the region through Boluda Towage and its maritime transport and logistics activities. It also opened new offices in Rotterdam in June 2026. Following completion of the planned acquisitions, Boluda Shipping expects its international network to comprise 21 maritime terminals and five rail terminals. The expanded infrastructure would support connections between short-sea shipping, rail transport and road distribution. Rotterdam is expected to play an important role in coordinating these services and connecting Northern European markets with the Iberian Peninsula, the Canary Islands and West Africa. For Boluda, adding Matrans would provide additional cargo-handling and storage capacity at a major European gateway. The terminal’s rail facilities could also support the development of multimodal transport services. Both the Matrans and Samskip acquisitions remain subject to the necessary approvals. Until the transactions are completed, the announced network expansion remains conditional.

articles.title: Cflow Provides Fish Handling System for Brønnbåt Wellboat
articles.summary: Brønnbåt Nord's largest wellboat to date will be equipped with a complete fish handling system from Cflow in Langevåg, on Norway's west coast. The solutions have been further developed to ensure good conditions for the fish, gentler handling…
articles.body: Cflow Provides Fish Handling System for Brønnbåt Wellboat Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 10, 2026 © Cflow Brønnbåt Nord's largest wellboat to date will be equipped with a complete fish handling system from Cflow in Langevåg, on Norway's west coast. The solutions have been further developed to ensure good conditions for the fish, gentler handling and efficient operations on board. With a cargo capacity of 5,000 cubic meters, the new wellboat can carry the equivalent of approximately 4.2 million salmon dinners in a single trip to the processing plant. The investment will help meet growing demand for wellboat capacity in Northern Norway. Brønnbåt Nord is owned by the aquaculture companies Salaks, Gratanglaks and Kleiva Fiskefarm. The vessel has been designed by NSK Ship Design in Harstad and will be built at Zamakona Shipyard in Bilbao, Spain, with delivery scheduled for 2029. The newbuild will feature battery-hybrid propulsion, an energy-efficient hull design and the capacity to produce up to 10,000 cubic meters of freshwater on board. The new vessel will be equipped with several further-developed Cflow solutions designed to ensure good water quality and greater control over the conditions fish are exposed to during transport and handling. Cflow's delivery includes complete systems for fish handling, water circulation and treatment, hygiene, automation and data logging. It also features high-capacity CO2 degassing systems, systems for regulating total gas pressure (TGP), and nanobubble generators from Cflow's partner Moleaer, which supply oxygen to the water. The nanobubble generators inject very small oxygen bubbles that remain in the water for longer, rather than quickly rising to the surface. According to Cflow, this enables more efficient use of oxygen compared with traditional venturi injectors. The vessel will be equipped with fish loading and unloading lines with a diameter of 600 millimeters (DN600), designed to handle high capacities during loading and unloading. This will enable efficient fish handling and shorter operation times, while keeping fish welfare a key priority. Cflow will also deliver piping systems designed for cleaning in place (CIP), without the need for dismantling. This will simplify cleaning procedures and help maintain good hygiene between operations. In addition, the vessel will be equipped with fish counters from Wingtech, adapted for different operations on board. The counters will record the number of fish during loading and unloading, and one of the counters will also be suitable for smolt counting. This will give the shipping company better control over the number of fish being handled. Cflow and Brønnbåt Nord previously collaborated on the battery-hybrid wellboat MS Caspian , delivered in 2024. Experience gained from that project has been carried forward into the development of solutions for the new vessel. Although the vessel will be built in Spain, approximately 40 per cent of the deliveries will come from Norwegian companies. For Cflow, based in Langevåg near Alesund, the contract means significant activity in the years ahead, helping to support local employment and further development of the company's technology expertise.

VIKING Life-Saving Equipment has signed a €23.8 million contract, through its Greek company VIKING Life-Saving Equipment Hellas, to supply seven new high-speed patrol vessels to the Hellenic Coast Guard. The contract was signed by Greece’s Minister of Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy, Vassilis Kikilias, at a ceremony at the Ministry in Athens, attended by Coast Guard officials and VIKING representatives. The seven vessels are of the VIKING Norsafe Magnar 1950 type and will be built entirely in Greece, one of five countries with VIKING’s manufacturing facilities. Each vessel measures 21.29 metres in length, reaches a top speed of at least 50 knots and has a range over 320 nautical miles. Each will operate with a six-person crew, carry at least 30 people, and be equipped with modern navigation and communication systems. Once in service, the vessels will support the Coast Guard’s core missions: surveillance of Greek waters, protection of the country’s maritime borders, fisheries control, and search and rescue. The contract also includes an option for up to seven additional vessels of the same type. Deliveries are scheduled to begin within six to twelve months, with vessels handed over in succession. At the signing, Minister Kikilias described the procurement as another decisive step in supporting the men and women of the Coast Guard. He said the goal is “to make their job easier, facing the challenges of today and tomorrow.” “We are honoured by the trust placed in VIKING by the Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy and the Hellenic Coast Guard. This contract builds on more than a century of boatbuilding expertise within VIKING, and on the skills of our team in Greece. Building these vessels locally reflects our commitment to Greek shipbuilding and to the people who protect lives at sea every day.” John Georgiadis, Tenders & Projects Director | Defense & Professional, VIKING Life-Saving Equipment. “This contract is significant both for our Defence & Professional business and for VIKING. It broadens the range of vessels we supply to the Coast Guard, and we are proud to earn that confidence.” Heidi Bjerge Nüsser, VP Defence Wind & Aviation, VIKING Life-Saving Equipment. The procurement is funded by the Public Investment Programme through the co-financed programme “Fisheries, Aquaculture and Sea 2021–2027. articles.title: Iran claims two oil tankers are burning in Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Tuesday, 10 November, that two oil tankers had caught fire following explosions while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz through routes not authorised by Tehran. According to a statement carried by Iranian news agency Tasnim, one of the vessels,...
articles.body: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Tuesday, 10 November, that two oil tankers had caught fire following explosions while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz through routes not authorised by Tehran. According to a statement carried by Iranian news agency Tasnim , one of the vessels, described as a supertanker, allegedly struck a naval mine, triggering an explosion and subsequent fire. The second tanker reportedly experienced a separate incident while attempting to cross the waterway under the alleged protection of US military aircraft. The IRGC claimed that both vessels had switched off their navigation and identification systems before attempting the passage. The tankers were subsequently left immobilised and burning near the southern coast of the strait, according to the statement. Iranian authorities did not disclose the names, flags or ownership of either vessel, while no details were provided regarding their crews, potential casualties or the extent of the reported damage. The circumstances surrounding the incidents, including the alleged US military involvement, have not been independently verified. Maritime security concerns continue The latest announcement follows a series of similar claims by Iranian authorities concerning tankers attempting to use routes that Tehran considers unauthorised. On 5 November, the IRGC reported that two oil tankers and a tugboat had caught fire in separate incidents in the Strait of Hormuz. Further claims involving vessels striking naval mines were made in the following days. With vessel identities remaining undisclosed, it is unclear whether the latest announcement refers to entirely separate incidents. The situation comes amid continued restrictions on commercial navigation through the waterway, which connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and remains a critical corridor for international energy shipments. Earlier this year, Iran established the Persian Gulf Strait Authority , introducing a framework requiring vessels to obtain authorisation before transiting the strategic passage. Commercial shipping has faced mounting security challenges in the region since the escalation of the conflict in late February. In October, the Singapore-registered container ship GFS Pride sank following a projectile strike near the Strait of Hormuz , while another Singapore-registered container vessel, GFS Giselle, sustained damage in a separate incident. The latest Iranian claims add to uncertainty surrounding maritime operations in the area, although independent confirmation of the reported tanker incidents remains outstanding.

articles.title: From basic wave data to trusted predictive decision support
articles.summary: What turns a wave measurement into a prediction your crew can trust?
articles.body: Branded Content November 10, 2026 · 41 minutes ago From basic wave data to trusted predictive decision support What turns a wave measurement into a prediction your crew can trust? Written in partnership with Miros 7 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Start with the operational question: Do you understand the wave conditions around your vessel during operations? Can the crew find the measurement when they need it? Can they explain what significant wave height and wave period mean for this vessel and this task? Source: Miros real-time WaveSystem dashboard showcase (AI Illustration) Author: Lars Ivar Leivestad, Commercial Manager at Miros Picture a vessel holding position offshore. The next operation has been carefully planned, the crew is briefed, and the weather forecast suggests conditions are within operational limits. But then the vessel starts moving more than expected. The sea looks much the same as it did earlier. Is this a temporary variation or a sign of changing sea conditions? Will it now impact the lifting operation, personnel transfer or equipment deployment about to begin? How can the crew make an informed decision about whether to proceed? Local, real-time sea state measurements can help. By providing an accurate picture of the sea conditions around the vessel, they help bridge the gap between forecasts and what is happening offshore. But having access to data is only the first step. The real value comes from understanding the measurements, connecting them to operational decisions and building more advanced capabilities as needs evolve. Start with the operational question: Do you understand the wave conditions around your vessel during operations? Begin with a task the crew recognizes. For a Chief Officer preparing a deck cargo transfer on a platform supply vessel, that might mean understanding the wave conditions along the vessel during the operation. Identify the question and the people who need the answer. One of our offshore vessel customers began with just such a need. They already had forecasts and experienced personnel, but wanted a continuous, measured real-time reference for the local sea state. The first installation used a single non-contact wave sensor, with significant wave height and wave period as the initial parameters. Forecasts remain part of planning. Real-time measurements add information about conditions at the measurement location. Before you add more data, decide what the first measurement is for. Name the decision it should inform. For the Chief Officer, that could be the call on whether to start the deck cargo transfer. Then set a first goal the team can check. Can the crew find the measurement when they need it? Can they explain what significant wave height and wave period mean for this vessel and this task? Are they using it in the go/no-go discussions you identified? Once the answer to each is yes, crew and management share a clear baseline. Know what the number represents: Is the sensor wrong, or are you comparing two different things? Say a larger wave passes the vessel while the significant wave height changes little. Significant wave height, commonly written Hs, is a statistical measure approximately corresponding to the average height of the highest third of waves. Individual waves can be higher. Wave period is the time between successive wave crests passing a fixed point. Displays can present it in more than one way, so confirm which period parameter yours shows. The measurement context is equally important. Identify the sensor location, the area or point it observes, the reporting interval and the quality information available. Understand how the system accounts for vessel motion. A downward-looking range measurement from a moving platform needs appropriate motion compensation to distinguish surface movement from sensor movement. A reading from one point on the vessel does not describe every point around the hull. Check the timestamp and the averaging period used for statistical parameters. Those details help distinguish a live display update from the passage of an individual wave. Ask the watch team to explain the parameter in relation to the task. Significant wave height, commonly written Hs, is a statistical measure approximately corresponding to the average height of the highest third of waves. Individual waves can be higher. The measurement context is important. Source: Miros varying sea condition illustration (AI Illustration) Build confidence through operational use: When the sea changes, what changes on the display? Give the team opportunities to compare measurements with conditions and vessel behavior during normal work. When a measurement seems surprising, review the observation, the parameter definition and the data quality together. In our customer’s initial experience, personnel compared wave readings with what they could see and feel. Over time, they began relating combinations of wave height and period to their vessel’s behavior. A Master and Chief Officer can bring that same learning into a briefing: the measured conditions, the planned task and the relevant operating limits. Recording the conditions and the vessel’s operating state gives later reviews something specific to examine. Visual agreement helps build familiarity, but technical verification is still necessary to confirm measurement performance. Confidence requires both reliable measurements and an understanding of their operational significance. Progress shows when people can explain what the readings mean for their work, identify gaps and raise questions that experience alone or the initial parameters do not fully answer. Add context when the question changes: Why can a familiar significant wave height accompany a different vessel response? Wave period and direction relative to heading can help explain the difference. Waves approaching the bow, beam or stern do not produce the same response in every case. Add directional information when it addresses a specific operational need. Surface current measurement can provide further context for a Dynamic Positioning Officer considering environmental conditions on a construction support vessel. It does not provide a current profile through the water column. This expansion requires the right measurement configuration. Combining X-band radar with a downward-looking wave sensor adds directional wave and surface-current information to the local wave measurements. Before interpreting directional data, confirm the reference frame and conventions in the system documentation. Wave direction must be understood in relation to the vessel’s heading and the operation. The key question: Can users understand and explain the purpose of each additional measurement? Confirm the required equipment, interfaces and data quality before introducing new parameters. Video clip: 3D vessel view 3D interface in Miros WaveSystem, showing where each wave measurement is taken. It brings each installed measurement source, its measurement area and the key wave values together in one intuitive display, providing a bird’s-eye view of the sea state data most relevant to safeguard operations. Source: Miros WaveSystem 3D vessel visualization Connect the waves with the vessel: Which approaching waves and associated motions would be useful to anticipate? Now bring measured vessel response into the discussion. Vessel design, size, loading condition, heading and operating mode all influence how a vessel responds to the sea. Wave height alone cannot describe the implications for every operation. For a service operation vessel preparing a gangway connection, relate the environmental conditions to vessel motions and the applicable equipment and operational limits. For a research or survey vessel recovering an instrument, connect the wave conditions with the motions affecting equipment handling. Assess these relationships in the context of the specific vessel and operation. Keep wave measurements, vessel motions and equipment performance distinct. Understanding one does not automatically establish the others. Identify the motion, such as heave, roll or pitch, and where on the vessel it matters. Measure or predict where it matters. Bring measured vessel response into the discussion. Vessel design, size, loading condition, heading and operating mode all influence how a vessel responds to the sea. Wave height alone cannot describe the implications for every operation. Source: Cable lay vessel, Adobe Stock Evaluate the prediction against actual outcomes: How do you know the prediction is right? Approach prediction with the same discipline as the initial measurements. Establish what is being predicted, how far ahead, under which conditions and with what level of uncertainty. Miros’ PredictifAI technology, for example, combines X-band radar observations of incoming waves, local downward-looking wave measurements and artificial intelligence. It provides deterministic predictions of waves and vessel motion, including when they will occur. The published prediction horizon ranges from seconds to a couple of minutes, depending on installation and operating conditions. Available predicted output depends on the installation. Motions influenced by dynamic positioning, navigation or crane operations cannot automatically be predicted from wave measurements alone. Compare predictions with subsequent measurements to assess their accuracy. Consider the timing and size of the event, the uncertainty involved and the conditions in which the comparison was made. Review the results with relevant personnel before deciding how predictions should support operations. The available prediction might support a critical phase of a lifting operation or a remotely operated vehicle (ROV) deployment. But the prediction horizon alone cannot establish suitability for an entire operation extending beyond it. Understanding the measurements helps users look beyond the “black box.” Confidence starts with reliable input data, but predictions must also demonstrate their accuracy and operational value. Video clip: PredictifAi traffic light display Miros’ PredictifAI technology combines X-band radar observations of incoming waves, local downward-looking wave measurements and artificial intelligence. It provides deterministic wave and vessel motion prediction, from seconds to a couple of minutes, depending on installation and operating conditions. Source: Miros PredictifAI traffic light display Make the information part of the watch The next watch should also be able to use and question the information. Integrate it into training, handovers, toolbox talks and operational reviews, ensuring its role within existing procedures is clear. Establish how personnel should respond when data is unavailable or unreliable. A Marine Operations Manager with access to the same measurements can discuss plans with the offshore team using a shared understanding of conditions. A Marine Superintendent can help integrate the technology into training and procedures, in line with the operator’s defined responsibilities. A Coast Guard vessel preparing to launch or recover a small boat must also consider local sea conditions and vessel motions in the context of the task. Prediction remains one input alongside forecasts, procedures, measured conditions and established operational limits. Qualified personnel retain responsibility for operational decisions. Back on board, the next operation still requires a decision. Better-informed discussions can start with a single trusted measurement, then build toward directional waves, surface currents, vessel response and prediction. Measure. Understand. Trust. Expand. Predict. One trusted measurement. One practical step at a time. Some organizations may benefit from a more comprehensive system from the outset. For those new to wave monitoring, the priority is to establish the value of the initial measurements before expanding. articles.summary: The South Korean city of Changwon is seeking to position the planned Jinhae New Port as a future hub for Arctic shipping, linking the major port development project with the region’s established shipbuilding, machinery, and defense industries.

(Source: Changwon city hall) The South Korean city of Changwon is seeking to position the planned Jinhae New Port as a future hub for Arctic shipping, linking the major port development project with the region’s established shipbuilding, machinery, and defense industries. The initiative reflects growing interest in the Northern Sea Route as a shorter alternative for trade between Asia and Europe. While the port is already under construction it will not begin opening its first terminals until the next decade, reflecting the long-term proposition of Arctic shipping. Jinhae New Port is a national infrastructure project designed to accommodate some of the world’s largest container ships. Plans call for 21 berths capable of handling vessels of up to 25,000 TEU and a 6.98 million-square-meter logistics hinterland. The first phase, comprising nine berths, is targeted to open in 2033. Changwon’s latest proposal is not to build a separate Arctic port, but to incorporate the potential shipping route into the development of Jinhae New Port and its surrounding industrial base. The city expects increased Arctic shipping to generate demand for ice-strengthened and polar-capable vessels , specialized ships, engines, propulsion systems, insulation materials, sensors and automated port equipment. It believes manufacturers in the Changwon National Industrial Complex could adapt existing capabilities in shipbuilding, machinery, robotics and defense to supply those markets. The strategy would give Jinhae a role extending beyond cargo handling, potentially making it a base for vessel equipment, maintenance, and other services in support of ships operating in polar conditions. That proposition differs somewhat from the one brought forth by neighboring Busan, South Korea’s established maritime and logistics center. Busan is positioning itself as an international maritime business hub, emphasizing shipping, logistics, maritime finance and related services. The distinction is also reflected in the central government’s broader plan for the southeastern region, which envisages Busan as a maritime business center and South Gyeongsang Province, where Changwon is located, as a supply-chain and manufacturing base. Changwon Mayor Kang Ki-yoon said the city wanted Jinhae, historically an important naval port, to take on a new role in the Arctic shipping era. He pledged close cooperation with the central government to establish the port as a source of economic growth for the region and the country. South Korea’s Arctic ambitions have gained momentum following the PanStar Acro’s round-trip voyage between Busan and Europe via the Northern Sea Route. The 2,758-TEU container ship returned to Busan on October 11 after a 50-day voyage, demonstrating that a South Korean container vessel could complete the journey. The commercial results, however, were less conclusive. The vessel departed on August 22 with just 737 TEU of loaded export cargo , alongside 202 TEU of empty containers, well below the roughly 1,300 TEU initially anticipated. It returned without loaded import cargo, highlighting the difficulty of securing freight in both directions. South Korean officials attributed the limited outbound cargo partly to the short period available to arrange bookings before departure. Whether that reflects an exceptional constraint of a pilot voyage or a more persistent challenge in attracting customers to the route remains unanswered. Seoul is targeting regular Arctic shipping services by 2030, although the route’s commercial viability, reliability, and operating costs still require further assessment. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Oil production has kicked off from BK-26 platform at Bach Ho field Source: Vietsovpetro Beating its planned start date by more than a month, the Vietnam-Russia joint venture Vietsovpetro has achieved its first oil flow from a wellhead platform at the Bach Ho field off the coast of Vietnam to boost its 2026 output amid natural field declines and strengthen the Southeast Asian country's energy security. articles.title: Suez return could limit November freight rate increases, Sogese warns
articles.summary: Container shipping lines may struggle to secure the full freight rate increases announced for November as more vessel capacity returns to the Asia–Europe trade through the Suez Canal, according to a new market report from Italian logistics company Sogese. In its November 2026 Europe Container Market Update, Sogese...
articles.body: Container shipping lines may struggle to secure the full freight rate increases announced for November as more vessel capacity returns to the Asia–Europe trade through the Suez Canal, according to a new market report from Italian logistics company Sogese. In its November 2026 Europe Container Market Update , Sogese highlights the growing gap between carriers’ announced rates and current market assessments. Although freight rates have recovered from their earlier declines, increasing vessel availability could limit further gains. The report also warns that the return to shorter Suez routings is progressing faster than improvements in schedule reliability, creating additional challenges for shippers and logistics operators. Freight rate increases face growing capacity pressure According to Drewry’s World Container Index , average container freight rates stood at US$4,389 per 40-foot container on 5 November, down from US$4,585 on 22 October. On the Asia–Europe trade, Shanghai–Rotterdam rates reached US$3,615 per 40-foot container, while Shanghai–Genoa stood at US$4,166. These assessments remain below the November Freight All Kinds (FAK) rates announced by major carriers. MSC filed rates of US$4,500 for North Europe and US$5,000 for the Western Mediterranean and Adriatic, while CMA CGM announced US$4,900 for the Western Mediterranean. Sogese believes carriers may secure only part of these increases as effective capacity expands. Andrea Monti, CEO and Managing Director of Sogese, said the market is increasingly moving away from disruption-driven pricing towards a period in which carriers’ capacity management will play a more important role. The report identifies the gradual return of Suez Canal transits as a key factor. Shorter voyages can release vessel capacity previously absorbed by longer routes around the Cape of Good Hope. However, the impact on freight rates will depend on whether shipping lines use this capacity to improve fleet efficiency or introduce additional sailings. As Container News recently reported , global freight benchmarks have already shown renewed weakness following their recovery in October. Schedule reliability remains a major concern Despite the return of capacity, operational reliability continues to present difficulties for shippers. According to Xeneta’s September schedule reliability assessment , only 4% of Far East–Europe vessel arrivals were on time during September, with average delays reaching 9.9 days. Sogese warns that shorter transit routes will not automatically resolve these disruptions. Changes to vessel rotations could also lead to overlapping arrivals and increased pressure on European container terminals. The report highlights differing conditions at Italian gateways. Between 8 October and 5 November, Shanghai–Genoa freight rates increased by 12.7%, compared with an 8.3% rise on Shanghai–Rotterdam. Meanwhile, rail capacity, inland connections and terminal congestion remain important factors in determining the total cost of transporting cargo. The return to Suez could also affect container equipment availability. Faster vessel rotations may reduce the number of containers needed to support the same cargo volumes, potentially creating regional equipment surpluses. Looking ahead, Sogese expects the normalisation of Suez Canal services to continue into 2027. However, the company cautions that security risks and ongoing network adjustments could delay a broader recovery in schedule reliability. For shippers preparing their 2027 contracts, the report recommends greater attention to routing flexibility, surcharge conditions and service performance rather than focusing exclusively on headline freight rates.

REUTERS/Stringer/File Photo Nov 10 (Reuters) – Renewed Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries since late October have reduced Russia’s oil refining capacity by about 30%, two industry sources said. Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries add to Moscow’s difficulties in addressing domestic fuel shortages as it ships diesel to international markets under an export deal with US President Donald Trump. Ukraine has stepped up strikes on Russian refineries since the end of October, when a ceasefire on attacks on energy facilities that Trump announced between Kyiv and Moscow failed to take hold. Ukrainian attacks disrupted operations and caused emergency situations at nine of Russia’s 35 major refineries over the past week, according to industry sources and officials. According to the industry sources, the combined daily nameplate capacity of Russian refineries affected by drone attacks since late October, including three major plants in central Russia, stands at around 300,000 metric tons, or 2.2 million barrels, compared with Russia’s total primary refining capacity of about 930,000 tons per day. At the end of October, Russian refineries were processing about 700,000 tons, or 5 million barrels, of crude per day, according to the sources. The sources estimate that the actual reduction in crude processing at Russian refineries could be up to 200,000 tons per day. The affected plants include refineries in Ryazan, Yaroslavl and the Volga region. On Monday, a Ukrainian drone struck the Kirishi oil refinery, Russia’s second-largest, in an overnight attack that set the refinery on fire, the governor of the Leningrad region said, adding that one woman had been killed in the attack. In an article published on Tuesday in the Russian daily newspaper Kommersant, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine was ignoring Trump’s calls to stop strikes on Russian energy targets. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said last week that Kyiv was continuing to launch attacks on targets associated with Russia’s oil sector in response ?to Russian strikes on energy targets. He said Ukrainian power ?plants, energy networks, heating systems and water supply systems ?were subject to constant attacks, and that Moscow had “refused the de-escalation steps that our partners talked about”. articles.summary: Liquefied natural gas loadings onto tankers from Qatar have picked up over the past few weeks, suggesting the major exporter is seeking to get more cargoes to the global market despite ongoing disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

Photo: RasGas By Stephen Stapczynski Nov 10, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Liquefied natural gas loadings onto tankers from Qatar have picked up over the past few weeks, suggesting the major exporter is seeking to get more cargoes to the global market despite ongoing disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. The number of LNG shipments departing Qatar’s Ras Laffan facility has ranged from 13 to 15 on a 10-day moving average basis so far this month, according to data from Bloomberg, Kpler and Copernicus. That’s up slightly from an average of about 11 in October, but still roughly half the pre-war pace. Still, the rise in loadings has yet to translate into a similar bounce in estimated eastbound traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — the waterway that links Qatar with Asia and Europe. Eleven laden Qatari LNG tankers exited in the 10 days through Nov. 8, according to Bloomberg and Kpler data. While the rate of crossings has remained broadly steady over the past month, it’s been common for there to be a mismatch between the figures for loadings and exits. Both rely on hard-to-verify data points, with most of the ships loading at Ras Laffan or transiting Hormuz not transmitting their locations. QatarEnergy, which operates the Ras Laffan facility, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Global energy markets including LNG and oil have been zeroed in on Persian Gulf loadings and flows through Hormuz, with the US-Iran war in its ninth month. Even though there has been a wave of speculation that Washington may seek an end to the conflict after a resounding Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections last week, dealing a setback to President Donald Trump’s administration, vessels transiting the waterway continue to be targeted in attacks. Trump met on Monday with Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, whose nation has served as a mediator during the war that began in February. After that, the US leader said further strikes on Iran wouldn’t be necessary, adding: “We’re just keeping it the status quo.” Any sustained increase in Qatari LNG supply reaching the wider market would offer some relief as colder winter weather in the Northern Hemisphere threatens to intensify competition between Europe and Asia for limited available volumes. European gas prices have retreated from highs reached in late October, but remain more than twice the level before the conflict began. While one of Qatar’s LNG tankers was attacked late last month, that hasn’t seemingly resulted in a drop in exports or Hormuz transits. Previous attacks had resulted in a slowdown of Qatari LNG flows through Hormuz. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: A consortium of Diamond Transmission UK (DTUK) and Japan’s Chubu Electric Power has been selected as the preferred bidder to acquire and operate...
articles.body: News November 10, 2026 · 1 minute ago Ofgem names preferred bidder for Dogger Bank B offshore transmission assets AB Adrijana Buljan Offshore Wind 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Dogger Bank Wind Farm A consortium of Diamond Transmission UK (DTUK) and Japan’s Chubu Electric Power has been selected as the preferred bidder to acquire and operate the offshore transmission assets connecting the 1.2 GW Dogger Bank B wind farm to the UK grid. The transmission system, valued at approximately £1 billion (around €1.2 billion) by the consortium, comprises subsea and onshore cables, an offshore converter station and an onshore converter station. The consortium will operate the transmission business for 25 years after acquiring the assets and receiving an Offshore Transmission Owner (OFTO) licence from the UK energy regulator. The preferred bidder appointment is part of Ofgem’s Tender Round 11 process. Ofgem launched the tender round in February 2024 and shortlisted four bidder groups in July that year. Ofgem appointed the consortium of DTUK and Chubu as the preferred bidder on November 5. Dogger Bank B, located approximately 130 kilometers off the UK’s east coast, is the second phase of the world’s largest offshore wind farm under construction, the 3.6 GW Dogger Bank Wind Farm, owned by the consortium of SSE Renewables, Equinor, and Vårgrønn. The second phase is currently under construction, with wind turbine installation underway . The Dogger Bank B transmission system uses high-voltage direct current (HVDC) technology to transmit electricity from the offshore wind farm to the National Grid. Its offshore converter station was installed in April 2024 by Saipem’s Saipem 7000 heavy-lift vessel. DTUK is wholly owned by Global Infrastructure Partners, part of BlackRock. Following the acquisition, the company will operate eleven UK OFTO projects with a combined capacity of almost 7 GW and a total transferred asset value exceeding GBP 5.5 billion (around €6.6 billion), according to the consortium. For Chubu, the Dogger Bank B project will be its third UK offshore transmission investment, following its participation alongside DTUK in the Walney Extension and Hornsea 1 OFTO projects. The Japanese utility said it would contribute its technical expertise in transmission systems while building experience in HVDC technology and the operation and maintenance of subsea transmission assets. November 10, 2026 Illustration of Golar’s FLNG units (Credit: Golar LNG) Techouse has secured a contract from Black & Veatch to supply heat recovery steam generation (HRSG) modules for Golar LNG's fourth floating liquefied natural gas (FLNG) project, with the system expected to reduce fuel consumption by 20-25% compared with conventional gas turbine-only systems. The contract covers two HRSG modules weighing approximately 1,000 tonnes each, along with supporting systems, Techouse announced on November 10. Techouse will deliver the equipment as a subcontractor to Black & Veatch, which is responsible for the FLNG topside solutions. The HRSG technology recovers heat from the exhaust of gas turbines used to drive compressors for LNG production, generating pressurised superheated steam that can be used to produce electricity through steam turbines and supply heat to the LNG process. Engineering and procurement will be managed from Techouse's offices in Norway, while its partner Alpha ECC will manufacture the HRSG units in Vung Tau City, Vietnam. The equipment will then be shipped to Himile Heavy Industries in China for assembly into complete HRSG modules. Work on the project is starting immediately, with delivery of the modules planned by the end of 2028. Techouse will also provide installation and commissioning support. “This is a large and strategically important contract for Techouse, for an energy recovery technology that we have delivered multiple times to similar offshore projects. We look forward to supporting Black & Veatch and Golar LNG in making this project a success,” said Svein Helge Pettersen, CEO of Techouse. The company previously supplied HRSG technology for FLNG Gimi and FLNG Esperanza, but the latest award marks its first contract to deliver complete HRSG modules to Black & Veatch/Golar LNG. On October 7, 2026, Golar LNG announced an agreement to acquire the LNG carrier Grace Dahlia from NYK Line, with the vessel intended for conversion into its fourth FLNG unit. The conversion project is targeting final redelivery in 2029.

articles.title: UK offshore supply chain looks overseas for growth
articles.summary: The UK’s offshore energy supply chain is increasingly looking overseas for new business as uncertainty surrounding domestic projects threatens investment, jobs and specialist engineering capacity, according to a new industry report. Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) found that just 35% of 60 companies surveyed were...
articles.body: Europe Offshore UK offshore supply chain looks overseas for growth Bojan Lepic November 10, 2026 0 204 1 minute read OEUK OEUK The UK’s offshore energy supply chain is increasingly looking overseas for new business as uncertainty surrounding domestic projects threatens investment, jobs and specialist engineering capacity, according to a new industry report. Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) found that just 35% of 60 companies surveyed were confident about their UK business prospects over the next 12 months. Meanwhile, 80% expect more future investment and growth to come from international markets. The findings form part of OEUK’s Supply Chain Report 2026, which examines the pressures facing engineering companies, manufacturers, vessel operators, logistics providers, and other businesses supporting offshore energy developments. The trade body identified approximately £123bn ($165.5bn) of potential UK offshore energy capital investment between 2026 and 2035 but warned that many projects remain uncertain. According to the report, 95% of companies surveyed believe they could expand capacity if domestic offshore activity increased. However, without commercially viable contracts and more predictable project schedules, suppliers risk redirecting personnel, equipment and investment to countries offering greater certainty. Oil and gas remains particularly important, with nine in ten surveyed companies deriving more than 20% of their revenue from the sector. OEUK warned that offshore wind, carbon capture, and other emerging energy markets have not yet generated sufficient activity to replace traditional oil and gas work at scale. Katy Heidenreich, OEUK’s supply chain and people director, called for continued investment in domestic oil and gas alongside renewable energy developments. The organisation also urged project developers to engage contractors earlier and provide clearer procurement schedules. OEUK cautioned that losing specialist offshore capabilities now could leave the UK increasingly dependent on overseas suppliers when future energy projects move into construction. articles.body: AIQ, Quartermaster Join Forces on AI-Powered Offshore Security Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 10, 2026 (Credit: AIQ) Abu Dhabi-based industrial AI company AIQ and US maritime intelligence firm Quartermaster have signed a strategic collaboration agreement to explore AI-enabled maritime safety and security solutions for offshore energy operations. The agreement, signed during ADIPEC 2026 in Abu Dhabi, will initially focus on the United Arab Emirates, with plans to explore opportunities across the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region and international markets. The collaboration will combine Quartermaster's SmartMast maritime sensor network with AIQ's expertise in offshore oil and gas operations, safety workflows and artificial intelligence. SmartMast provides vessel detection, identification and maritime awareness independently of AIS data, GNSS or satellite systems. According to Quartermaster, the technology has recorded more than three million detections across 25 countries. AIQ has already deployed its SMARTi AI-enabled computer vision solution on scores of vessels operating in the UAE. Under the agreement, the companies will evaluate joint commercial opportunities and demonstrate integrated solutions for monitoring and protecting offshore platforms, pipelines and subsea infrastructure. The proposed applications also include detecting unauthorised vessels and suspicious maritime activity, identifying safety incidents and supporting data-driven risk assessments that could help offshore operators secure more favourable insurance outcomes. The companies intend to expand their collaboration beyond the UAE as the partnership develops. Established in 2020 as a joint venture between G42 and ADNOC, AIQ provides artificial intelligence solutions for the energy sector, with Presight, a G42 company, holding a majority stake.

articles.body: Asia Middle East Tankers Asyad and MOL sell ageing LR2 for $63m Adis Ajdin November 10, 2026 0 245 1 minute read Michael Hatje / Marine Traffic Michael Hatje / Marine Traffic Oman’s Asyad Shipping and Japanese shipping giant Mitsui OSK Lines (MOL) have agreed to sell their jointly owned LR2 product tanker, extending the Omani owner’s campaign to cash in on ageing tonnage. The Muscat-listed company disclosed that the 2009-built Haima , held through a 50:50 joint venture with MOL, has been sold for OMR24.3m ($63.2m). The transaction is expected to generate a gain of approximately OMR19m ($49.4m) at joint venture level, with Asyad’s share amounting to OMR9.5m ($24.7m), subject to final closing adjustments and accounting treatment. The 110,077 dwt tanker has been part of the company’s fleet since construction. The buyer has not been named, and completion is expected during the second half of November. The latest disposal follows Asyad’s September agreement to sell three older tankers for a combined OMR68.44m ($178m). That package involved the 2011-built VLCCs Seeb and Samail , alongside the 2008-built MR tanker Al Amerat . The company has been recycling capital from older ships into a substantial fleet expansion programme. Its recent investments include eight MR product tanker newbuildings at HD Hyundai, all backed by five-year charter arrangements, as well as additional VLCCs at Hanwha Ocean. Asyad has said it will continue evaluating disposals of older vessels as part of its fleet renewal programme. articles.body: Container News participated as an official Media Partner in the international maritime conference “Shipping at the Historic Turning Point of 2030”, organised by SK Congress on 5 November 2026 at the InterContinental Athens. The event brought together shipping executives, shipowners, institutional representatives, diplomats and maritime professionals to examine the challenges and developments shaping the future of global shipping, with discussions covering maritime leadership, port infrastructure, alternative fuels, geopolitical developments and emerging technologies. According to the organisers, attendance exceeded initial expectations, reflecting strong interest across the maritime community. Participants represented shipping companies, ports, shipyards, cruise operators, energy suppliers, technology businesses and other sectors of the maritime industry. The conference opened with a welcome address by Sotiria Katsimicha, President of SK Congress, followed by institutional greetings. Among those attending were Stefanos Gikas, Greece’s Deputy Minister of Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy, Stavros Avgoustides, Ambassador of Cyprus, Julie Lymberopoulos, Ambassador of Panama, and George Alexandratos, President of the Hellenic Chamber of Shipping. Member of the European Parliament Eliza Vozemberg also addressed the conference through a video message. Industry discussions and key themes The conference featured four main panel discussions, beginning with international maritime leadership. Participants included Andreas Tsavliris of Tsavliris Group, Chrysanthi Stefanou, Managing Director of Bright Navigation, Loukas Sigalas, CEO of Minoan Lines, and George Vernicos, Founder and President of Vernicos Yachts. A second panel focused on ports, shipyards and marinas, bringing together representatives from the Port of Volos, the Greek Marinas Association, Celestyal and CrediaBank. Discussions addressed a segment of the maritime industry closely connected to infrastructure development, investment and operational requirements. Geopolitical developments and their implications for global shipping were also examined in a dedicated presentation by Dimitris Abatzidis, Maritime Risk and Compliance Manager at MarineTraffic Operations. The industry’s energy transition formed another central theme, with a panel dedicated to alternative fuels and green infrastructure. Representatives from J.H.I. Steamship, Bunker Holding, the Hellenic Shipbrokers Association and Investment & Finance Ltd participated in the discussion. The final panel explored artificial intelligence and automation, featuring participants from Venergy, BCA College, Xplisi Technologies and the University of the Aegean. The programme also included a presentation by internationally recognised space scientist Stamatis Krimigis, who addressed developments in space technology. The conference was presented by Nigel Lowry, Athens Correspondent of Lloyd’s List, while Giannis Moutsios, journalist and news presenter at MEGA News, and Greta Christofilopoulou, Shipping Editor, moderated the panel discussions. The event also attracted media coverage, including from Greek public broadcaster ERT, which featured the conference in its television news coverage. Container News participation (From left to right): Alexandros Itimoudis-Geopolitical Analyst, Antonia Saratsopoulou- Managing Editor, Giannis Nikolakis- Managing Director Container News was represented at the conference by Giannis Nikolakis, Managing Director, Antonia Saratsopoulou, Managing Editor, and Alexandros Itimoudis, Geopolitical Analyst. As an official Media Partner, Container News supported the initiative, which provided an opportunity for industry professionals to exchange perspectives, strengthen connections and explore developments affecting the maritime sector. The conference concluded with a networking reception, bringing together representatives from shipping companies, ports, shipyards, energy and technology businesses, alongside institutional and diplomatic participants.

articles.title: Norway’s IMO proposal: will more flexibility create a functioning surplus market?
articles.summary: Norway has proposed a substantial redesign of the IMO Net-Zero Framework, combining additional Surplus Units for zero- and near-zero fuels, five-year banking and broader use of surplus across both compliance tiers. The package offers a credible compromise, but its success depends on a difficult question: can the same...
articles.body: Norway’s IMO proposal: will more flexibility create a functioning surplus market? in International Shipping News 10/11/2026 Norway has proposed a substantial redesign of the IMO Net-Zero Framework, combining additional Surplus Units for zero- and near-zero fuels, five-year banking and broader use of surplus across both compliance tiers. The package offers a credible compromise, but its success depends on a difficult question: can the same surplus market deliver affordable compliance while providing a sufficiently high and predictable reward for investing in cleaner fuels? Ahead of ISWG-GHG 23 and MEPC 85, Norway has submitted two closely related proposals, ISWG-GHG 23/2/5 and ISWG-GHG 23/2/6, seeking to address concerns with the IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF). Rather than abandon the existing architecture, Norway proposes modifying its incentives and flexibility mechanisms while retaining the two-tier GHG Fuel Intensity (GFI) compliance system. The proposal has several interesting features. It would reward the use of qualifying zero- and near-zero GHG fuels and technologies (ZNZs) through additional Surplus Units (SUs), rather than relying exclusively on monetary rewards from an IMO fund. It would extend SU validity from two to five years, allow SUs to balance both Tier 1 and Tier 2 deficits, and with that also replace Remedial Units with Voluntary Contribution Units (VCUs) as an alternative compliance route. However, the package also places considerably more responsibility on the SU market. Surplus would no longer be merely an instrument for transferring excess compliance between ships. It would become a central determinant of the financial support delivered to ZNZ users. Our assessment is that Norway has identified the right problems, but has not yet demonstrated that its proposed market design can solve them under both normal and exceptional fuel-market conditions. What Norway’s IMO proposal is about Under Norway’s suggested 2030 trajectory, the Base Target would require a 4.8% GFI reduction against the IMO reference value of 93.3 gCO₂e/MJ, while the Direct Compliance Target would require a 17.8% reduction. These correspond to absolute GFI thresholds of 88.8216 and 76.6926 gCO₂e/MJ respectively. Similar to previous proposals, ships above the Base Target would face both Tier 1 and Tier 2 deficits. Ships meeting the Base Target but remaining above the Direct Compliance Target would face only Tier 1 deficits. Norway retains the contribution rates of USD 100/tCO₂e for Tier 1 and USD 380/tCO₂e for Tier 2. The significant change is that SUs could be used against either tier. Previously, the framework restricted transferred or banked SUs to Tier 2 compliance, leaving Tier 1 dependent on contribution (RU) payments. Norway also proposes a technical multiplier for qualifying ZNZ use. Importantly, this is not the same design as China’s proposed energy multiplier. Norway would leave the vessel’s attained GFI unchanged and award additional SUs according to the verified emissions avoided by ZNZ fuels and technologies. The multiplier would start at 1.25 in 2029, decline to 1.10 in 2030, reach 0.30 in 2033 and remain at that level until 2036, subject to review. Norway proposes strengthening Brazil’s suggested Base Target trajectory by 20% to compensate for some of the additional compliance benefits. The objective is understandable: give ZNZ users a more predictable quantity of compliance value while preserving incentives for actual fuel switching. However, as FuelEU Maritime shows, predictability in the number of units is not the same as predictability in their market value. 1. Can a ship generate SUs while failing direct compliance? Starting with an interesting nuance, Norway intentionally allows for SU generation from ZNZ even if the respective ship is not compliant. Under proposed Regulation 36, ordinary SUs would continue to arise when a ship’s actual compliance balance is positive. Additional ZNZ SUs, however, would be issued independently of whether that ship meets the Direct Compliance Target. Norway argues that a ZNZ incentive should not disappear simply because a ship cannot yet operate with a sufficiently high share of qualifying fuel. To understand the effect, consider an illustrative ship consuming 1 PJ of energy in 2030. We use the fuel intensities in Norway’s own analysis: conventional fuel at 95.48 gCO₂e/MJ and qualifying ZNZ fuel at 19 gCO₂e/MJ. If the vessel uses ZNZ fuel for 15% of its annual energy consumption, its actual attained GFI would be 84.008 gCO₂e/MJ. This is below the Base Target, but still well above the Direct Compliance Target of 76.6926 gCO₂e/MJ. The ship would consequently have a Tier 1 deficit of approximately 7,308 tonnes CO₂e. Using the avoided-emissions reference implied by Norway’s fleet calculations, its ZNZ consumption would simultaneously produce approximately 12,260 additional SUs at the proposed 2030 multiplier of 1.10. After using sufficient units to balance its own deficit, the ship could retain or transfer approximately 4,952 SUs, despite not having achieved direct compliance through its actual fuel mix. Under the same assumptions, a ship using only ZNZ and conventional fuel reaches a net positive unit position at approximately 11.9% ZNZ energy use, well before it physically meets the Direct Compliance Target. That is important as the IMO would be permitting ships to become net suppliers of compliance units without outperforming the Direct Compliance Target in their actual GFI. One may argue that refusing ZNZ incentives to every ship with a physical deficit could discourage early adoption, especially where qualifying fuel is unavailable in sufficient quantities. However, the IMO must at least distinguish between SUs created through actual outperformance and SUs created as an additional policy incentive. Both may be legitimate, but they are not economically or environmentally identical. If agreed, this distinction should be visible in the GFI Registry, including separate reporting of issuance, internal use, transfers, banking and cancellation as it will be crucial to assess the ‘real’ progress towards achieving the environmental targets. 2. How much additional surplus could enter the market? Norway’s analysis assumes annual energy consumption of approximately 10 EJ for the relevant fleet, consistent with its cited range of 9.1–10.6 EJ from the IMO comprehensive impact assessment. Using Norway’s assumed fuel intensities, and applying its actual 2030 targets and multiplier, we calculated three illustrative fleet scenarios: The second scenario is particularly interesting. At a 5% ZNZ energy share, the fleet would generate 40.87 million additional SUs, compared with 28.34 million tonnes of remaining Tier 2 deficits. If those units were available and allocated first to the more expensive Tier 2 obligations, approximately 12.52 million units would remain to address less expansive (below USD 100) Tier 1 deficits or be banked. The third scenario illustrates how competition from other low-GHG fuels changes the balance further. With the same 5% ZNZ share and an additional 5% of energy supplied by a non-ZNZ pathway at 25 gCO₂e/MJ, the hypothetical fleet would have no Tier 2 deficit at all. Its remaining demand would be Tier 1, while the multiplier would still generate 40.87 million SUs priced at below USD 100 in the SU market. Please note that the assumption that every ship uses the same fuel mix is deliberately simplified, and the distribution of fuel use matters greatly. In this context, it is important to recognise that a single fleet-average ZNZ uptake assumption cannot establish that Norway’s proposal will produce a stable SU market. The market structure can be very different if not only considering the aggregated fuel mix but a more detailed distribution of fuel usage across different market participants. The relevant modelling must distinguish between early adopters generating large volumes of SUs, partial adopters using bonus units internally, and conventional-fuel ships creating demand. It must also account for other low-GHG fuels that improve actual GFI without qualifying for the multiplier. Norway’s own analysis recognises that additional SUs may substitute for physical emissions reductions and therefore proposes strengthening the targets. But its 20% adjustment is based on high-level assumptions. It is not yet evidence that the additional issuance would remain environmentally neutral across materially different patterns of ZNZ uptake. 3. Two targets, two contribution prices, but only one SU market Norway wants to preserve two GFI targets while allowing the same SU to balance deficits under either tier. The idea is largely politically motivated as it allows the framing of voluntary units rather than the less accepted Tier 1 RU payment. While this expands the potential market for surplus, it must be noted that Tier 1 and Tier 2 buyers won’t have the same willingness to pay. A ship facing a Tier 2 deficit compares SU purchases with the USD 380/tCO₂e contribution alternative. A Tier 1 buyer compares them with an alternative costing USD 100/tCO₂e. Therefore, a company with only Tier 1 exposure would have little reason to pay USD 150 or USD 200 for an SU that could be replaced by a USD 100 contribution unit. A company with Tier 2 exposure, by contrast, might still find an SU attractive at those prices. Consequently, opening Tier 1 to surplus does not automatically create additional demand at the same prices as Tier 2. This means the market could behave very differently depending on the relative quantities of outstanding Tier 2 deficits and available SUs. Where Tier 2 demand is abundant, SU prices could remain materially above USD 100. Where higher-value demand has largely been satisfied, further supply would increasingly compete against the lower Tier 1 contribution alternative. At the same time, the USD 100 rate should not be mistaken for a guaranteed floor. On the contrary, if surplus availability exceeds demand and the anticipated value of banking, prices could fall below it. Norway’s design therefore increases the usability of SUs, but cannot guarantee their value. However, the two-tier structure may still be desirable. It provides a potentially more acceptable alternative to direct compliance and helps contain extreme compliance costs by outbalancing oversupply with additional but lower priced demand. 4. Norway’s own fuel economics reveal a potential incentive mismatch The central commercial concern becomes clearer when we examine the fuel prices Norway uses to justify the multiplier. In ISWG-GHG 23/2/5, Norway compares conventional fuel costing USD 11/GJ and emitting 95.48 gCO₂e/MJ with a non-ZNZ low-GHG fuel costing USD 25/GJ at 25 gCO₂e/MJ. It then considers two ZNZ fuels, both at 19 gCO₂e/MJ, but priced at USD 45/GJ and USD 65/GJ respectively. Under those assumptions, switching from conventional fuel to the non-ZNZ pathway costs approximately USD 199 per tonne of physical emissions avoided. Switching to the cheaper ZNZ fuel costs approximately USD 445 per tonne avoided before accounting for the additional SUs. The ZNZ fuel therefore needs a substantial additional incentive to compete. Norway illustrates the solution using an assumed SU price of USD 200/tCO₂e. At a multiplier of 1.25, its cheaper ZNZ pathway becomes approximately competitive with the non-ZNZ alternative. Under the corresponding avoided-emissions accounting, the resulting abatement cost falls to roughly USD 200/tCO₂e. But what happens if the SU price is USD 100 rather than USD 200? A considerable scenario if oversupply of SUs results in unlocking lower priced Tier 1 demand. The effective abatement cost of the same ZNZ fuel rises to approximately USD 323/tCO₂e avoided, while the non-ZNZ alternative remains around USD 199 under the assumed fixed fuel prices. The multiplier has not changed. The number of units awarded has not changed. Yet their financial value is no longer sufficient to close the illustrated cost gap. This exposes a weakness in relying on SUs as the principal ZNZ incentive. Norway’s own example needs an SU price close to USD 200 to make its lower-cost ZNZ fuel competitive. But the additional Tier 1 demand created by its proposed flexibility mechanism is anchored to a USD 100 contribution alternative. For high-cost fuels, the distinction between a fixed multiplier and a fixed monetary reward is material. The former determines the quantity of units received but leaves the market to determine the value realised, creating uncertainty that is suboptimal for financing new fuel production or propulsion technology. More certainty in higher SU prices can, for example, be created by either increasing the costs of the voluntary contributions or establishing more ambitious targets. An interesting additional point has been raised by an IMarEST submission. The proposal warns that using SU prices as a measure of incentive requirements creates a feedback risk: the incentive itself changes SU supply and therefore influences the price being used to value it. For example, if Norway’s multiplier succeeds in increasing qualifying ZNZ use, more additional SUs enter the market. If that extra issuance depresses SU prices, the incentive delivered to future ZNZ users weakens. Of course, demand and banking also change, but it is a pricing mechanism that should be modelled. 5. Five-year banking: what FuelEU and the Strait of Hormuz teach us Norway proposes extending SU validity to five calendar years after the year of issuance, compared with two years under the original framework and there is a good economic argument for doing so. Short expiry periods can force surplus holders to sell at unfavourable prices even where their units could have value against future tightening targets. Longer banking gives companies greater flexibility and can connect current compliance values with expected future scarcity. However, banking can also carry the consequences of an unusually favourable generation period into subsequent years. FuelEU Maritime offers a relevant market example. BetterSea’s volume-weighted monthly surplus index declined from EUR 106.52/tCO₂e in July 2026 to EUR 84.09 in October. The volume-weighted end-of-month price reached EUR 73.72/tCO₂e on 30 October. This decline occurred despite continued trading activity and the ability to bank surplus compliance balances. It does not prove that banking failed: without knowing what prices would have been in its absence, that conclusion would be unjustified, but it demonstrates is that banking does not override the economics of generating new compliance. The market has been heavily influenced by the elevated conventional bunker-price environment associated with disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. Where conventional fuels become more expensive relative to certain biofuels, the incremental cost of generating compliance can fall sharply. For example, at the current moment (November 2026), the FuelEU compliance-generation cost is approximately EUR -19/tCO₂e for Bio100 in the Netherlands against MGO, compared with EUR 176/tCO₂e against VLSFO. The differences demonstrate an important economic point: the same alternative pathway can face very different generation costs depending on the fuel being displaced. When low-cost sources can satisfy sufficient demand, more expensive generators (SU sellers) cannot assume that the market will compensate their higher production costs. For Norway’s proposal, the implication is straightforward. Imagine that an external fuel-price shock makes certain compliance-generation pathways unusually inexpensive for two or three consecutive years. Companies may generate additional units, retain some for future use and sell others into the market. Once fuel prices normalise, the accumulated inventory does not disappear. Under a five-year validity regime, those units could continue meeting obligations during later reporting periods. This may support early generators, but it could also reduce the need for fresh alternative-fuel use in subsequent years. A risk currently omnipresent under FuelEU Maritime. The risk becomes more significant if the same period also sees substantial issuance of multiplier-generated SUs. Norway recognises the danger of excessive accumulated stocks and argues that a finite five-year period offers a compromise between short-term price pressure and unlimited banking. What is missing is evidence that five years is the appropriate period under realistic oversupply and market-shock scenarios. A robust assessment should compare two-, three- and five-year validity under different fuel-price trajectories, including a prolonged period of low-cost surplus generation followed by normalisation. It should examine outstanding unit stocks by issuance year, their use against subsequent deficits and their impact on demand for newly generated compliance. It should also consider whether ordinary SUs and additional multiplier-generated SUs necessarily require identical banking treatment. Our assessment: Norway’s direction is sensible, but the market design needs a stronger test Norway’s proposal deserves support as a serious attempt to reconcile several competing requirements. It preserves the two-tier compliance structure, replaces remedial units with voluntary contributions by allowing SUs for Tier 1 compliance, and rewards qualifying ZNZ use through additional SUs. However, the success of the SU market is of utmost importance for achieving the ultimate GHG reduction targets particularly in Norway’s proposal, which is why we request a more rigorous assessment of the interaction between these mechanisms to fully understand their impact on the SU market. Three questions should be answered before the rules are finalised: First, how many ordinary and multiplier-generated SUs would be issued under plausible fuel-uptake scenarios, and how would that issuance affect actual fleet emissions? The IMO should model both concentrated and dispersed ZNZ adoption, competing non-ZNZ pathways and different levels of fuel availability. The proposed strengthening of the GFI targets should be validated against those outcomes. Second, what is the likely relationship between SU supply and the remaining Tier 1 and Tier 2 deficits? Norway’s broader eligibility can improve market flexibility, but Tier 1 demand is anchored to a USD 100 contribution alternative. It cannot automatically sustain the approximately USD 200 SU value used in Norway’s own illustration of ZNZ competitiveness. Third, how resilient would the market be to prolonged external fuel-price shocks? A five-year bank may protect sellers against temporary weak prices, but it can also carry a large inventory of inexpensive compliance into later years. The IMO needs stress tests and transparent inventory data, not only assumptions about future target tightening. The wider lesson from FuelEU Maritime is that the regulatory value assigned to compliance is not necessarily the price realised in the market. That price emerges from the economics of the available generation pathways, the demand still requiring compliance, the willingness of generators to offer units and the value of retaining them for future years. Norway’s proposal improves the ways in which surplus can be created and used. The remaining task is to demonstrate that those improvements produce a market capable of supporting the fuel investments the IMO wants to encourage. After all, a successful compliance market should be judged by whether the price signals it generates support actual emissions reductions and the development of the fuels required for deeper decarbonisation. Source: BetterSea 2026-11-10 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Ahead of ISWG-GHG 23 and MEPC 85, Norway has submitted two closely related proposals, ISWG-GHG 23/2/5 and ISWG-GHG 23/2/6, seeking to address concerns with the IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF).
Rather than abandon the existing architecture, Norway proposes modifying its incentives and flexibility mechanisms while retaining the two-tier GHG Fuel Intensity (GFI) compliance system.
The proposal has several interesting features.
