Manuel Diaz, director general of the Latin...
articles.body: Hormuz, global shocks open door for Latin America as reliable supplier – APLA in International Shipping News 10/11/2026 Latin America should use the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz and other global shocks to present itself as a reliable, peaceful supplier of energy and petrochemicals and to build regional supply chains, the head of the region’s petrochemical and chemical association said. Manuel Diaz, director general of the Latin American Petrochemical and Chemical Association (APLA), said that current geopolitical woes could be “an enormous opportunity” for Latin America. “The competitor is on the other side. Hormuz gives us a key element of reliability, both as a producer and as a supplier of raw materials, and that is something we must seize in Latin America. Why the conflict in Hormuz happened is irrelevant. What matters is that there was a problem, and there will be others, because not everything can be resolved once and for all,” said Diaz. “That is where the region’s great opportunity lies: in saying, ‘We are here.’ In fact, the first contract signed to export liquefied natural gas [from Argentina] was with Germany. They need a reliable supplier – not because they don’t have reliable partners, but because of what happened to them [too much dependence on Russian natural gas].” Diaz spoke to ICIS on the sidelines of the group’s annual meeting in Buenos Aires last week. TROUBLED WORLD MAY BOOST LATAM Diaz went on to say that the troubles-turned-opportunities for Latin American chemicals “don’t depend only on” who is in the US White House, but on the increasing conflicts and crisis happened in the past intense decade. “First, we had the pandemic, then Russia and Ukraine, and now Hormuz. And before that, October [2023] in Palestine. It’s not straightforward, but I think it’s a good opportunity, and I think one of the countries to benefit from this is clearly Brazil,” said APLA’s director general. “For sure, Latin America can be described as a region of peace. We have a lot of difficulties, a lot of things to improve, but we are a society of peace,” he said, highlighting that industry-disruptive armed conflicts are unlikely to emerge in the region. As he hinted though, Latin America has some social unresolved woes which put a break in overall activity – rampant inequality keeps millions on survival budgets, unable to jump into consumerism. Diaz said he was “very convinced” that the industry would shift towards regional supply chains rather than moving “so many atoms, so many molecules” between continents. He declined to choose between Brazil’s model of tariffs and antidumping duties and Argentina’s market opening under President Javier Milei, which is causing havoc in industrial sectors, with many closures taking place. Diaz said Brazil, which he placed on the 10 global chemicals sectors, was defending a sector of global relevance, rather than practicing protectionism. Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has hiked import tariffs for chemicals and implemented several antidumping duties (ADDs) to cushion domestic producers. “Competition today isn’t between companies. We’re no longer competing with the competitor next door. Globally, the competition in chemicals is a competition between governments’ public policies. And, ultimately, it isn’t going to be black or white. It will surely be something grey,” said Diaz. “If we’re talking about protectionism, the US also applied tariffs, and I don’t consider the US a protectionist country. It’s the reality we’re living through right now, and we must adapt to what’s happening in the world, a world which is changing – Europe, which always had a surplus in chemicals, is not having a good time and is reinventing itself. I think this will bring about a reinvention of the industry globally.” ARGENTINA DIFFERENT VIEWS Diaz is an Argentinian national and APLA’s headquarters are located in Buenos Aires. Therefore, the annual meeting organizers played in home turf after six years of absence, as Argentina nearly went to the abyss and back – a more normalized economy allows for more of the events side of business. It was a well-attended APLA annual meeting, after the poor attendance numbers registered in 2025 in Mexico’s Cancun. APLA’s membership includes a variety of players in the chemicals chain, but it is chemicals producers who carry most of the weight in the trade group. While Diaz said Brazil’s protectionist policies were a natural response to the global state of affairs – overcapacity and record low prices for long – he did not address Argentina’s Milei industrial policy, which is not being benign for the sector. Other players in the chain, however, had no qualms to summarize what Milei’s three years in office have meant for chemicals. In an interview with ICIS, an executive at Argentine distributor Simpa said it can be asserted by now that industry comes on the other side of the economic adjustment as clear losers. High-cost and globally uncompetitive production plants across most manufacturing sectors have been shutting down recurrently. On the winning side, the less job-intensive, export-oriented oil and gas, agriculture, and mining, among other few exceptions. For most, the shock therapy is still deeply felt and consumerism remains depressed. “Whoever sells plastic is doing badly; whoever sells textiles is doing badly; whoever sells construction materials is doing badly. When there are no pesos available [as the cabinet tries to keep inflation in check, soaking up pesos], there’s no economic activity, so with fixed costs high and demand weak, companies were cutting prices to win business,” said Simpa’s Adrian Schwartz in the interview. “At the end of the month, everyone sees they only sold 10-15% less than usual, but that they sold everything at zero margin,” he added, ending with an equally bleak forecast for the future of industrial firms. He told that some converter Simpa customers have told him that they plan to close their plants if Milei wins the October 2027 election – giving a measure of the scarring last three years in which the opening to overseas, cheaper imports was bound to hurt local players – and it did so exactly as expected. “They [the converters] are not going to hold out for four more years of fighting [if Milei wins again],” concluded Schwartz. articles.body: LNG shipping stocks: Post-election selloff in International Shipping News 10/11/2026 The UP World LNG Shipping Index fell 9.35 points (4.07%) to close at 220.05, caught in a broad risk-off week — the S&P 500 had its worst week since the April 2025 crash, down 2.68%. The decline was near-universal: breadth was just 3:18, the median fell 6%, and the weighted index (wUPI) dropped 5.5%. Two forces combined after the US mid-term elections — a weakening administration that eased geopolitical risk premiums (and so energy prices), and a tech/AI-led equity selloff that dragged shipping down in tandem. European gas prices fell 17% on higher Qatari loadings and softer Asian demand. Only three names rose: Nakilat led (+10.12%, a third straight gain on US contracts and reduced geopolitical threat) and Excelerate added 4.1% after strong quarterly results (new Bahamas contract, extended Petrobras charter to 2038, updated Colombia/Iraq start dates). The fallers were led by Tsakos (−16.7%) and BP (−11.6%), with Chevron −9.73%, the Japanese trio down 7–9.5%, and Shell, NFE, FLEX LNG and Pan Ocean each off around 8%. Dynagas (−6.9%) was pressured by European sanctions concerns and a need for a new insurer. Spot tanker rates diverged sharply — Atlantic surged to $55,250, Pacific $32,750 — reflecting Europe’s new pull. UPI & SPX The UP World LNG Shipping Index, which tracks 21 listed LNG shipping companies, lost 9.35 points (4.07%) to close at 220.05 points, while the S&P 500 index lost 2.68%. The chart below illustrates the performance of both indices with weekly data. Week 45-2026: Chart of the UP World LNG Shipping Index with S&P 500 (Source: UP-Indices) Broader View The fall in the UPI was quite significant, and two key related factors played a part: 1. the US mid-term elections and 2. developments on the stock markets. One might conclude that the first factor alone is the key driver, but it is more accurate to break this down into two factors. The weakening of the current US administration has reduced concerns about geopolitical consequences and, consequently, lowered energy commodity prices, while also dampening expectations and optimism around AI and its infrastructure. Shares linked to technology and various forms of shipping fell in tandem. The UPI thus fell four per cent, with a median movement of -6 per cent and the weighted index (wUPI) down 5.5 per cent. Trading volume rose as expected, but not significantly. The ratio of rising to falling constituents was 3:18. As Reuters reported in its weekly round-up, gas prices fell, particularly in Europe, where they recorded a 17 per cent decline. Lower Asian demand and increased LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz have made Europe a more attractive destination for cargoes, increasing supply offers there, said Martin Senior, head of LNG pricing at Argus. “Prices have fallen over the past week, partly because of an apparent shift in tone towards de-escalation from Trump and increased expectations of Qatari supply, with loadings well above half of capacity,” Senior said. European storage remains a key source of support, with inventories currently 74 per cent full – well below the seasonal average – leaving a smaller buffer heading into winter, said Aly Blakeway, head of Atlantic LNG at S&P Global Energy. Regional appetite for LNG will be partly capped by China’s stable coastal LNG inventories, secured Bangladeshi supplies, and limited Pakistani spot demand. However, geopolitics will be the main price mover, particularly following the U.S. mid-term elections, with both increased attacks and de-escalation on the table, said Ronald Pinto, principal LNG and gas analyst at Kpler. Spot charter rates for LNG tankers have increased. Reflecting Europe’s greater attractiveness, the Atlantic is $55,250 per day, and the Pacific is $32,750 per day, according to Spark Commodities. Constituents Only three companies grew, and one posted double-digit growth. Nakilat (QSE: QGTS) led the gains, rising for the third week in a row by 10.12%. It thus returned to the low level of the spring months and the high level of the summer months. After the American contracts and the reduction of the geopolitical threat (not the tension), cautious optimism prevails. The second-largest growth was 4.1% and belongs to Excelerate Energy (NYSE: EE), which broke through the sideways trend after its quarterly results. The results brought information about a new Bahamian contract (from Q1 2027 via Jamaican infrastructure and from mid-2028 a new FSU directly in the Bahamas). Updated the start dates of FSRU contracts for Colombia (Q1 2027) and Iraq (Q2 2027). The contract with Petrobras (FSRU Sequoia) was also extended until 2038. LNG trading is playing an increasingly important role. Both companies’ volumes were significantly above average. The last positive result was the symbolic growth of Korea Line Corporation (KRX: 005880), which amounted to 0.21%. The price tried to rise during the week but fell back, so the last two weekly results are the same, creating temporary additional support within a broader sideways trend. The biggest loser was Tsakos Energy Navigation (NYSE: TEN), which fell 16.7%. The decline pushed it below the current sideways movement, but it stopped at the spring peak’s closing price and slightly corrected the drop. The second double-digit decline of the week was bp (NYSE: BP), which fell 11.6%. It thus fell from its peak back to the summer sideways-growth zone. Two Japanese companies fell by 9 per cent: “K” Line (TSE: 9107; -9.5%) and Mitsui O.S.K. Lines (TSE: 9104; -8.1%) both fell from their peak prices to the bottom of their side band, with “K” Line even closing below it. A third Japanese company, NYK Line (TSE: 9101), also fell to support, losing 6.8%. The decline in the Japanese market affected all three more than other factors. Chevron (NYSE: CVX) also fell 9%, or 9.73% to be precise. It also stopped at the spring price level after erasing three weeks of growth, and so far it has returned to the range it left three weeks ago. Four companies have lost 8%, and that is the only thing that unites them. Shell (NYSE: SHEL) fell more than 8.6%, but it remains the best performer among the oil and gas trio. It is still above spring prices, and the edge of the September-October mini-band stopped the decline. New Fortress Energy (NASDAQ: NFE) corrected its growth from the week before last by a decrease of 8.74%, but as a result, its candle is positive thanks to the long shadow and small body in the upper part – lower prices were rejected this time. Flex LNG (NYSE: FLNG) fell 8.14% and traded in the $ 27- $ 24.5 range. The last 8% decline belongs to Korean Pan Ocean (KRX: 028670), and the price is on the border of two consecutive price levels. Golar LNG (NASDAQ: GLNG) fell to the lower level of the spring correction, losing 6.9%. This correction was followed by a 20% growth in the spring, which is unlikely now. Rather, a return to spring 2025 prices with a lower limit of $40. Dynagas LNG Partners (NYSE: DLNG) is dominated by concerns about the impact of European sanctions on Russian gas. The partnership reported needing a new insurance provider. The price returned to the 2024 level after a 6% drop. COSCO Shipping Energy Transportation (SS: 600026) lost 5.4%. Capital Clean Energy Carriers (NASDAQ: CCEC), which is also sideways, fell by five per cent. The remaining companies that lost less than 2% by telegraph: ALNG (OSE: ALNG) held on to the upper limit of the sideband despite a 1.8% drop. MISC (KLSE: 3816) started the week with growth, but ended with a 1.7% loss. Exmar (EBR: EXM) continues to move sideways, losing 1.3% during the week. ADNOC Logistics & Services (ADX: ADNOCLS) fell 0.73%. Crystal Ball Qatar remains on the sidelines among the losers of this conflict, yet its actions over the past few days have boosted market optimism. Its efforts to honour its commitments and fulfil its orders are undoubtedly a significant boost to its customers. US producers are seeking to capitalise on the resulting vacuum by accelerating capacity expansion as supplier diversification takes place. Price is no longer the sole criterion, and even Bangladesh has announced that it has signed a long-term contract with a US producer. Whilst the coming winter months will bring increased uncertainty and a scramble for gas – partly due to the uncertain geopolitical situation, with a significant risk of further US strikes on Iran – we expect the situation to stabilise and adapt in the spring, primarily through the diversification of suppliers. Source: By Tomas Novotny, UP-Indices.com 2026-11-10 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: A Chinese Survey Vessel Spent 53 Hours Over the SEA-H2X and EAC-C2C Cables
articles.summary: Fifty-Three Hours Inside a Twenty-Nine Mile Box From October 30 to November 1, a Chinese research and survey vessel spent approximately 53 hours inside a 29 nautical mile box over the SEA-H2X and EAC-C2C cable routes in the northern South China Sea. It covered about 226 nautical miles at a median of 5 knots, with ...
articles.body: A Chinese Survey Vessel Spent 53 Hours Over the SEA-H2X and EAC-C2C Cables in International Shipping News 10/11/2026 Fifty-Three Hours Inside a Twenty-Nine Mile Box From October 30 to November 1, a Chinese research and survey vessel spent approximately 53 hours inside a 29 nautical mile box over the SEA-H2X and EAC-C2C cable routes in the northern South China Sea. It covered about 226 nautical miles at a median of 5 knots, with 39 course changes over 45 degrees and 12 short stops. That is a back-and-forth line pattern with station-keeping. It is not a vessel drifting, holding position, or waiting. Partway through, the vessel went dark for about four hours on October 31 and resumed transmitting 13 nautical miles north of where it stopped. EO imagery caught it on station on November 1 at 03:02 UTC, directly above the SEA-H2X route. It returned to its home berth at Nansha, Guangzhou, on November 3. It Had Been There Six Days Earlier The loiter was not isolated. On October 24 to 26, the same vessel held position 3 to 6 nautical miles from the APG and SJC2 routes, going dark for 5 hours and again for 9 hours and 19 minutes while barely moving. Two visits to two separate cable corridors inside eight days, with dark periods inside both, is a sequence rather than a coincidence. The AIS Status Does Not Match the Behavior One detail separates this from ordinary survey work. Across all 230 recorded positions, including the stops, the vessel’s AIS navigational status read under way using engine. It never used restricted manoeuvrability, which is the status survey vessels set when they have equipment deployed and cannot manoeuvre freely. The vessel has signalled that condition before, just not through AIS status. Earlier this year it used the destination field instead, broadcasting “KEEP CLEAR OF ME 3NM” in May and “KEEP CLEAR OF ME 2NM” in July and August. Those are gear-in-water warnings. During the October and November loiters, no such warning appeared. The vessel either had nothing in the water, or chose not to say so through the channel that would have recorded it. It has also gone dark for 10 to 14 hours at a time around the Paracels and off Hainan since August. Who Owns It The vessel is a 117-meter research and survey vessel built in 2023, owned, operated, and managed by a Chinese institute whose fleet consists of this one hull. It is not sanctioned, but Windward rates it as high risk. Its dimensions match the 117.2-meter survey ship that the Guangdong Institute of Intelligent Unmanned Systems ordered from CSSC’s Guangzhou Shipyard International in 2021, specified with DP2 station-keeping, multibeam sonar and more than 600 tonnes of scientific payload. The Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Shenyang Institute of Automation established the institute in Nansha in 2019 as its Guangzhou deep-sea base, co-built with the Guangzhou municipal government. The two jointly develop 6,000-meter AUVs and 7,000-meter ROVs. The Shenyang Institute of Automation has been on the U.S. Entity List since 2022 for supporting military applications. So the vessel conducting the pattern belongs to an institute whose specialty is deep-sea robotics, backed by a parent institution restricted by the United States. Which Cables, and Whose The ownership of the four cables involved matters to the assessment. SEA-H2X is co-owned by China Mobile, China Unicom and Converge ICT, and lands in China, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand. A Chinese vessel surveying it is unremarkable on its face. EAC-C2C is different. It is Telstra’s alone, and it lands in China, Japan, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan. APG and SJC2, the subject of the earlier loiter, carry Taiwanese, Japanese, Korean and Southeast Asian traffic between them. What Slow Straight Lines Over a Cable Usually Mean Running slow, straight, overlapping lines across a corridor for two days is how cable routes are surveyed with hull-mounted multibeam sonar. The pattern in the track is the pattern that method produces. What raises the question beyond route mapping is the owner. The U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission reports that China is developing hibernating cable cutters that could be pre-placed on an adversary’s cables, and confirms a 4,000-meter cable cutter built by a state shipbuilding research centre. Pre-placement is not a route-data problem. It requires getting to the cable itself, which is what deep-sea ROVs and AUVs are built to do. On November 2, Yomiuri named four Chinese vessels for stopping over Taiwan’s cables. This vessel is not among them. What Can and Cannot Be Said AIS cannot show what a vessel had in the water. No survey is confirmed, no equipment deployment is established, and nothing here demonstrates interference with any cable. What the record does show is specific. A survey vessel owned by a deep-sea robotics institute returned twice in eight days to cable corridors carrying Taiwanese, Japanese, and Korean traffic, ran a survey-pattern track over two of them for 53 hours, went dark inside both loiters, and did not set the AIS status that would have marked the work as a survey. Windward assesses that profile as consistent with mapping these routes. Confirming more than that would require evidence that AIS does not carry. Source: Windward 2026-11-10 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: It covered about 226 nautical miles at a median of 5 knots, with 39 course changes over 45 degrees and 12 short stops.
That is a back-and-forth line pattern with station-keeping.
It is not a vessel drifting, holding position, or waiting.

articles.body: MMI Daily Iron Ore Index Report November 10 2026 in Chinese iron ore and steelmaking prices 10/11/2026 Iron ore futures and spot prices were broadly under pressure today. DCE most-traded closed at 684.0 yuan/mt, down 0.51% from the previous close, and all eight major Qingdao port quotations declined. The 61%, 58% and 65% port indices fell 3, 1 and 4 yuan, respectively. The seaborne 61% index eased to USD 91.35/dmt, the 65% held at 107.60, and all 12 brands edged lower. Grade spreads moved differently across markets; one-day changes do not establish a shift in blending trends. Physical balances still constrain a sustained rebound. Latest Chinese arrivals rose 33.30% WoW while global shipments fell 7.89%, with voyage lags potentially explaining the divergence. Existing ten-port stocks increased 643,600 mt from the previous period and surveyed daily hot metal fell 4,800 mt. Higher arrivals require mill buying and port absorption, but there is not yet a basis to state that current inventories have already risen further. A cautious, range-bound near-term view remains appropriate. A steady high-grade seaborne index and lower freight offer some buffer, while declining futures and spot prices and limited incremental demand restrain upside. Better orders and margins accompanied by sustained restocking could strengthen support; needs-based buying and slow absorption of arrivals could leave ore prices fluctuating under pressure. articles.title: Asia–Mediterranean freight pricing: The costs beyond headline rates
articles.summary: Asia Mediterranean freight rates are entering a new adjustment period in November, with higher published tariffs and renewed surcharges adding complexity to the cost calculations facing cargo owners and freight forwarders. Recent announcements from MSC and Maersk point to different approaches. MSC has raised its...
articles.body: Asia Mediterranean freight rates are entering a new adjustment period in November, with higher published tariffs and renewed surcharges adding complexity to the cost calculations facing cargo owners and freight forwarders. Recent announcements from MSC and Maersk point to different approaches. MSC has raised its published Freight All Kinds (FAK) rates for the second half of November while extending the geographical application of piracy risk and Suez Canal surcharges. Maersk, meanwhile, has announced a new Peak Season Surcharge (PSS) from Far East Asia to Mediterranean destinations, following the withdrawal of its previous PSS across the trade in September. The distinction matters because the carriers are not announcing equivalent pricing measures. MSC’s published FAK rates provide a basis for calculating specified additional charges, while Maersk’s PSS represents one component of its broader freight pricing structure. Comparing the two announcements directly would therefore give an incomplete picture of the cost facing a shipper. Asia Mediterranean freight rates: MSC’s November adjustments MSC’s revised FAK rates announced on 29 October apply from 15 November until further notice, but not beyond 30 November 2026. They cover shipments from Far East ports to Northern Europe, Mediterranean destinations and the Black Sea. A comparison with the carrier’s previous tariff announcement for 1–14 November reveals different levels of adjustment across destination regions. For a 40-foot dry or high-cube container, the published FAK rate from the Far East to the West Mediterranean increases from US$5,000 to US$5,300, representing a 6% rise. The Adriatic follows the same pattern. The increase is more pronounced for the East Mediterranean, where the rate rises from US$5,100 to US$5,700, equivalent to approximately 11.8%. For the Black Sea, the published rate moves from US$5,300 to US$5,900, an increase of approximately 11.3%. These changes show that MSC’s November pricing adjustment is not uniform across the region. The larger increases for the East Mediterranean and Black Sea create a wider difference between the published rates for those destinations and the West Mediterranean. However, the figures represent announced FAK tariffs for successive validity periods, rather than observed changes in the prices ultimately paid by customers. They do not establish how much cargo will move at the published levels or how individual contracts and bookings will be affected. The broader market context is also relevant. According to a Freightos market update published by Container News on 4 November , Asia–Mediterranean spot rates had increased by approximately 23% over the preceding month, while the benchmark stood at US$4,375 per FEU following a weekly rise of 3%. Forwarders nevertheless remained uncertain whether carriers would succeed in implementing further planned increases. That distinction is important. Published tariff increases demonstrate carriers’ pricing intentions, while freight market indices provide a separate indication of prevailing market conditions. Neither measure, considered alone, establishes the final cost of an individual shipment. The additional charges behind MSC’s published rates The structure of MSC’s tariff provides a clearer illustration of the difference between a headline freight rate and a price calculated after specified additional charges. According to the carrier’s 29 October pricing announcement , its published FAK rates already include the Global Fuel Surcharge (GFS), set at US$266 per TEU for November, and the applicable Emission Control Area (ECA) surcharge, listed at US$15 per TEU for Mediterranean destinations. These components should not be added a second time when calculating the cost from the published FAK figure. Other charges remain applicable separately. For Mediterranean destinations, MSC lists a Carbon Limitation Surcharge (CLS) of US$20 per TEU and a Carbon Review Surcharge (CRS) of US$133 per TEU. The carrier also applies a Piracy Risk Surcharge (PRS) of US$55 per TEU and a Suez Canal Surcharge (SCS) of US$36 per TEU, subject to the relevant geographical and effective-date conditions. Together, those four separately identified charges amount to US$244 per TEU, equivalent to US$488 for a 40-foot container. For a qualifying 40-foot shipment to a West Mediterranean base port, the published FAK rate of US$5,300 would rise to an illustrative US$5,788 after adding the four identified surcharges, assuming all are applicable. For a qualifying East Mediterranean shipment, the corresponding calculation produces US$6,188, based on a published FAK rate of US$5,700 and the same US$488 in identified additional charges. These amounts are not final freight quotations. They exclude any further applicable terminal handling, local, out-port or other charges and depend on the relevant tariff conditions for the shipment concerned. The calculation nevertheless demonstrates why the published FAK rate alone does not necessarily represent the full amount payable under the carrier’s tariff. MSC extends existing risk charges rather than raising their levels A further distinction concerns MSC’s 4 November announcement on piracy risk and Suez Canal surcharges. As Container News reported on 7 November , MSC extended the geographical application of both charges to the remaining Mediterranean and Black Sea ports, with effect from 15 November. The announced amounts remain US$55 per TEU for the PRS and US$36 per TEU for the SCS. MSC had already introduced these charges for selected East Mediterranean and Black Sea destinations in September, a development covered by Container News at the time . The carrier subsequently expanded the geographical coverage in October , before announcing the latest extension in November. The November development therefore represents a further geographical extension, rather than an increase in the stated surcharge levels. This is significant for cargo owners because the effect depends on the destination and whether the relevant charge was already applicable. For shipments to ports previously covered, the November announcement does not, by itself, establish an additional increase in the PRS or SCS amount. For newly covered destinations, however, the extension brings the two charges into the published tariff structure from the specified effective date. The distinction between a change in the amount charged and an expansion in the number of shipments potentially subject to that charge is central to understanding the latest tariff developments. Maersk brings back its peak season surcharge Maersk’s latest announcement follows a different pricing sequence. In its 12 August advisory , the carrier announced that its PSS would no longer apply to shipments from Far East Asia to North Europe and the Mediterranean from a Price Calculation Date of 1 September 2026. On 4 November, Maersk announced a new PSS for Far East Asia–Mediterranean shipments , effective from a Price Calculation Date of 23 November. The new tariff is US$750 for 20-foot containers and US$1,500 for 40-foot and 45-foot containers. The destination scope includes a broad range of Mediterranean markets, including Greece, Italy, Spain, Türkiye, Egypt and other countries specified in the announcement, as well as certain European destinations served through Mediterranean discharge ports. The latest measure restores a substantial PSS component after the September withdrawal. However, the US$1,500 level for a 40-foot container is not unprecedented. Maersk had announced the same amount during an earlier adjustment in June , before subsequent revisions and withdrawals. Unlike MSC’s published FAK announcement, Maersk’s November PSS notice does not provide a corresponding base ocean freight rate for a particular origin-destination pair. It is therefore not possible to calculate a comparable total Maersk freight amount from the PSS announcement alone, or to conclude that Maersk’s complete freight offering is more expensive than MSC’s. Suez uncertainty remains part of the pricing environment The latest pricing announcements also arrive as container carriers continue to adjust their operating networks around the Red Sea and Suez Canal. Some services have been announced for a return to Suez routing, while security concerns and operational uncertainty continue to affect other parts of the network. MSC explicitly refers to piracy risk around the Arabian Peninsula and its effects on vessel operations and transit routes when explaining the wider application of its PRS and SCS. However, the available announcements do not establish a direct causal relationship between individual Suez routing decisions and the November FAK increases or PSS changes. The two developments should instead be viewed as parallel features of a market in which operational arrangements and pricing conditions remain subject to change. Nor does the existence of a Suez-related surcharge establish that every shipment subject to the charge will necessarily move through the canal. Determining that would require shipment-specific routing and applicable tariff information. What Asia Mediterranean freight rates mean for shippers For cargo owners and freight forwarders, the immediate implication is that headline rate comparisons require greater attention to the components included in each carrier’s offer. MSC’s announcements make it possible to distinguish between charges already incorporated into the FAK rate and those listed as additional. Maersk’s announcement, by contrast, identifies a PSS that must be considered alongside the applicable freight offer and its terms. The comparison also depends on timing. MSC’s revised FAK validity period begins on 15 November, while Maersk’s newly announced PSS applies from a Price Calculation Date of 23 November. The dates are not interchangeable, and the relevant booking conditions must be checked before applying either tariff to a shipment. Container size, origin and destination ports, commodity exclusions, local charges and the treatment of surcharges within a specific quotation can all affect the amount payable. The distinction is particularly important when evaluating changes in transport costs over time. A rise in a published FAK rate, the introduction of a surcharge and the expansion of an existing surcharge to additional destinations are three different pricing developments, even when they occur within the same month. The November announcements demonstrate how those mechanisms can operate simultaneously across the Asia–Mediterranean trade. They provide evidence of higher announced MSC FAK rates, a wider geographical application of MSC’s existing risk-related charges and the renewed application of Maersk’s PSS. What they do not establish is a single market-wide increase in realised freight costs. For shippers, the more meaningful comparison remains the total applicable quotation for the same cargo, equipment, route and shipment period, rather than the headline freight rate or an individual surcharge considered in isolation.
takeaways: Recent announcements from MSC and Maersk point to different approaches.
MSC has raised its published Freight All Kinds (FAK) rates for the second half of November while extending the geographical application of piracy risk and Suez Canal surcharges.
Maersk, meanwhile, has announced a new Peak Season Surcharge (PSS) from Far East Asia to Mediterranean destinations, following the withdrawal of its previous PSS across the trade in September.

articles.body: Europe Offshore Energean taps Njord Survey for North Sea decom work Bojan Lepic November 10, 2026 0 170 1 minute read ODE Asset Management ODE Asset Management Swedish marine survey specialist Njord Survey has secured a contract from Energean to undertake post-decommissioning seabed surveys at three gas fields in the southern North Sea. The contract covers Wenlock, Garrow, and Kilmar, where survey work will assess the seabed following the removal of platforms and associated subsea infrastructure. Njord will carry out geophysical and environmental surveys across the former platform locations and pipeline routes, using multibeam echosounders, side-scan sonar, underwater cameras and environmental sampling equipment. The findings will be compared with earlier surveys to assess the impact of decommissioning activities and support Energean’s final reporting to UK regulators. Njord plans to deploy its own survey vessels, equipment and personnel for the work. Financial details and the execution schedule were not disclosed. Energean has already made substantial progress with its decommissioning programme in the region. In September, the company confirmed that the topsides and jackets at Garrow and Kilmar had been removed during a campaign involving Petrodec’s OBNA jackup vessel. The operation involved approximately 3,373 tonnes of offshore infrastructure, while removal of the Wenlock platform was scheduled for October. Garrow and Kilmar are located within the Southern North Sea Special Area of Conservation, making environmental monitoring an important part of the close-out process. articles.body: Containers Europe Greater China Operations Ports and Logistics Maersk boxship knocks down crane at Yantian Adis Ajdin November 10, 2026 0 1,752 1 minute read Source: WeChat Source: WeChat A Maersk-operated containership has brought down a ship-to-shore crane at China’s Yantian port after striking the structure while berthing. The incident involved the 366-m-long, 15,516 teu Maersk Cincinnati , which hit the crane at berth 12 of the Shenzhen terminal at around noon local time on November 9. Images and videos shared across Chinese social media show the crane collapsed towards the container yard, with sections of the structure lying alongside the vessel. The extent of the damage remains unclear, with no confirmed reports of injuries or details of any disruption to terminal operations. The Singapore-flagged, 2024-built boxship was operating voyage 645W on the Gemini Cooperation’s Asia-North Europe NE3 service. AIS data placed the vessel at Yantian on Monday, with the ship still alongside on Tuesday. It had been scheduled to depart on November 11 for Ningbo and Shanghai before heading to Tanjung Pelepas in Malaysia and onward to Europe. Strong winds may have played a part in the accident. Shenzhen’s meteorological authorities issued a monsoon warning at 6.10 am on Monday for Yantian and surrounding waters, with gusts of force 8 or above forecast. Chinese shipping sources have pointed to sudden gusts during the berthing manoeuvre, although the cause of the collision has yet to be established. Neither Maersk nor the terminal operator has provided a detailed account of the incident. Yantian was the scene of a similar accident in September 2024 when a quay crane collapsed onto the 1,730 teu MSC Riona at berth two, temporarily halting operations. No injuries were reported in that incident. Splash reported in October that GCC had added two 8,600 ceu car carriers at Changhong, bringing its orderbook at the time to 22 ships. The latest four vessels increase that programme by another 34,400 vehicle spaces and push the delivery schedule into 2031. GCC’s expansion has gathered pace since Mediterranean Shipping Company acquired Oslo-listed Gram Car Carriers in 2024 in a transaction worth around $700m. The Aponte-controlled group subsequently took the company private, with Gram adopting the Global Car Carriers name earlier this year. articles.body: Environment Europe Operations Regulatory New UCL tool flags food security risks from shipping emissions rules Bojan Lepic November 10, 2026 0 180 1 minute read Port of Riga Port of Riga The International Maritime Organization’s proposed shipping decarbonisation measures could disproportionately increase the transport costs of essential food imports, particularly for countries dependent on shipments of bulk cereals, according to new research from University College London (UCL). Researchers at UCL’s Shipping and Oceans Research Group have launched an online tool examining how different versions of the IMO’s Net-Zero Framework (NZF) could affect maritime transport costs and traded goods prices through 2050. The NZF Impact Tracker includes a dedicated food security section covering eight essential food groups, allowing countries to identify commodities most exposed to higher shipping costs. The analysis indicates that unprocessed cereals are particularly vulnerable because their relatively low value and high volume make freight a larger component of their delivered cost. Countries heavily dependent on imported cereals could consequently face greater increases in food transport costs than those importing higher-value products. Earlier research involving UCL identified Papua New Guinea, Haiti, Yemen, Solomon Islands and Liberia among countries particularly vulnerable to food security pressures associated with higher import costs. Separate IMF research found that inflation in small island developing states is nearly twice as responsive to international food commodity price shocks as in other economies. UCL’s new tracker covers 136 coastal countries, including 26 least developed countries and 36 small island developing states. The findings arrive ahead of the IMO’s MEPC 85 meeting later this month, where governments will continue negotiations over shipping emissions regulations and measures to protect vulnerable economies. articles.body: Carbon Capture Usage & Storage November 10, 2026 · 1 hour ago Seabed monitoring starts at UK CCS project to prepare for CO2 injection NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Sonardyne Six lander systems have been installed at the Northern Endurance Partnership (NEP) project, the UK's first commercial-scale offshore carbon capture and storage (CCS) project, to monitor the seabed before CO2 injection starts. Sonardyne, a Kraken Robotics company, reported the start of baseline environmental and passive seismic monitoring at the project, following the deployment of the six seabed lander systems at the Endurance CO2 store, in the Southern North Sea, about 150 kilometers off the coast of Teesside. The monitoring landers will support the long-term measurement, monitoring and verification (MMV) program for offshore CO2 storage by helping establish the robust, repeatable data needed to monitor the reservoir integrity effectively over time. Three autonomous environmental monitoring landers designed and built by Sonardyne and three co-located TIAMAT passive seismic monitoring systems from K.U.M. are collecting baseline data on seawater chemistry, currents, seabed conditions and passive seismic activity before future CO2 injection operations begin. This will support continued monitoring across the storage lifecycle. “Confidence in offshore CO₂ storage starts with good data. By delivering and deploying these environmental and micro-seismic monitoring systems, and managing their ongoing operation and data retrieval, Sonardyne is supporting a key part of NEP’s MMV programme at Endurance," said Stephen Auld , Business Development Manager for Custom Projects at Sonardyne. “For offshore CO₂ storage, that continuity matters. Long-term assurance depends on reliable data gathered across the full storage lifecycle, not a single point-in-time measurement — a role that draws directly on our experience in seabed-resident monitoring, acoustic communications and offshore integrity monitoring.” NEP, a joint venture of BP, Equinor and TotalEnergies, is delivering CO2 transportation and storage infrastructure centred on the Endurance store, which is about 1,000 meters beneath the seabed, as part of the East Coast Cluster decarbonization program across Teesside and the Humber. Storage is expected to start in 2028, making it the first operational CCS project in the UK. The initial phase is expected to see up to 100 million tons of CO2 stored in the Endurance aquifer over a 25-year period. “The deployment of these monitoring systems is a great example of the expertise and innovation that is helping to deliver CCS in the UK. Establishing a robust environmental and seismic baseline before operations begin, is a vital part of our long-term monitoring programme, providing the data required to demonstrate the safe and secure storage of CO₂ over time," said Mike Stephen , Head of Technical at NEP. articles.body: Greater China Offshore Renewables China Energy Engineering wins offshore wind EPC contract Bojan Lepic November 10, 2026 0 408 1 minute read Bureau Veritas Bureau Veritas China Energy Engineering’s Guangdong Electric Power Design Institute has won an engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contract to deliver offshore electrical infrastructure for two wind farms totalling 800MW off China’s Guangdong province. The award, confirmed by National Energy Group, covers the Jiangmen Chuandao I and II offshore wind developments, each with a planned capacity of 400MW. The Chinese contractor submitted a bid of RMB1.0267bn ($144m), according to an earlier tender announcement. The final contract value has not been separately disclosed. The scope includes engineering and design work, equipment procurement, fabrication, transportation, offshore installation, and commissioning of a 500kV offshore booster station and a reactive-power compensation station. The contractor will also undertake associated electrical infrastructure work and coordinate interfaces with the separately procured export cable package. The two wind farms are located approximately 62 km and 68 km offshore Jiangmen, with Chuandao II occupying waters between 39 and 45 metres deep. The turbines will collect power through 66kV subsea cables and transmit it to the offshore booster station, where the voltage will be increased to 500kV. Electricity will then pass through an offshore compensation station before reaching the landing point near Taishan and connecting to the onshore grid. The shared transmission infrastructure is designed to accommodate both developments, with the export system featuring two 500kV submarine cable circuits. articles.body: Tidewater Q3 Revenue Rises 5.3% as Offshore Vessel Day Rates Strengthen Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 10, 2026 Copyright Piter2121 Adobe Stock Tidewater Inc. reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $360.4 million, up 5.3% sequentially, as improving offshore support vessel (OSV) day rates and utilization supported earnings growth. The company also completed a $500 million acquisition in Brazil and issued an optimistic outlook for 2027, citing strengthening offshore activity and tight vessel supply. Net income for the quarter ended September 30 reached $17.5 million, compared with a loss of $800,000 in the corresponding 2025 period. Adjusted EBITDA totaled $140.1 million, while operating cash flow reached $75.2 million and free cash flow was $90.9 million. Average realized vessel day rates increased 3.7% sequentially to $23,775, while weighted average leading-edge term contract rates jumped 12.5% to $27,373, suggesting continued pricing momentum across the global OSV market. "Third quarter 2026 revenue and gross margin nicely exceeded our expectations driven by continued strength in day rates and utilization," said Quintin Kneen, Tidewater President and CEO. Gross margin reached 46.8%, exceeding company expectations by approximately one percentage point. A significant development during the quarter was Tidewater's completion of its $500 million all-cash acquisition of Wilson Sons Ultratug Offshore (WSUT), substantially expanding its presence in Brazil, a key offshore oil and gas market. Tidewater expects to substantially complete integration of the acquired business by early 2027. For the first nine months of 2026, revenue totaled $1.03 billion, compared with $1.02 billion a year earlier, while net income declined to $45.3 million from $114.8 million. Despite improving market conditions, Middle East geopolitical tensions continue to pressure operating expenses. Tidewater expects approximately $19.8 million in conflict-related costs during 2026, of which $8.7 million is recoverable from customers. The company updated its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $1.43 billion to $1.44 billion, with gross margins between 47.5% and 48.5%. Looking ahead, Tidewater projects 2027 revenue of $1.70 billion to $1.75 billion and gross margins of 51% to 53%, reflecting expectations for continued demand across offshore drilling, subsea construction, engineering, procurement, construction and installation (EPCI), and production support. Kneen pointed to improving offshore investment confidence and limited available vessel supply as drivers of future growth. "Broad-based confidence in the offshore cycle continues to improve," he said. Tidewater also repurchased approximately $25 million in shares since its previous earnings announcement, leaving $475 million authorized for additional repurchases.

articles.title: Oil Prices Slide as Trump Signals Pause in Iran Strikes
articles.summary: Oil prices fell on Tuesday, extending losses from the previous session after US President Donald Trump downplayed the need for additional military action against Iran "at this point," easing fears of sustained supply disruptions from the Middle…
articles.body: Oil Prices Slide as Trump Signals Pause in Iran Strikes Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 10, 2026 © Corona Borealis / Adobe Stock Oil prices fell on Tuesday, extending losses from the previous session after US President Donald Trump downplayed the need for additional military action against Iran "at this point," easing fears of sustained supply disruptions from the Middle East. Brent crude futures LCOc1 declined 1.7% to $90.99 a barrel at 0759 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures CLc1 fell 1.8% to $85.20 a barrel. Both benchmarks had fallen about 2% in the session. Brent settled down 5.85% in the previous session after sliding to its lowest since August 31. Trump said on Monday he plans to hold off on new military strikes against Iran for the time being after appeals from countries in the region, including from Qatar's prime minister in White House talks. Trump, in a Reuters interview and a later appearance in the White House press briefing room, said he plans to keep up a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz for now. "The market continues to prioritise President Trump's more conciliatory tone toward Iran since the midterms," said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade. "While attacks on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz are still occurring, they have not escalated in a way that has forced a fresh risk premium into the market," he said. On the supply side, OPEC oil output rose in October, a Reuters survey found, led by gains in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iraq despite continued constraints on exports. Brent has retreated about 22% from the six-month high of $118 it touched on October 30 as fears that Trump might step up attacks on Iran following the US midterms have eased, however there is still concern shipping could be disrupted. "Despite the recent selloff, prices are unlikely to fall below $90 per barrel for Brent without more durable signs of de-escalation and a US-Iran deal," Gregory Brew, a senior analyst with Eurasia Group said in a note. "At the same time, risks to shipping remain high, as Iran continues to attack vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz," Brew said. Elsewhere, Russian and Ukrainian officials planned to meet on Tuesday for two days of US-brokered talks - their first since February - after Trump suggested last week that a broad peace deal was possible in their 4-1/2-year-old war and could incorporate Europe's security. (Reuters - Reporting by Noel John in Bengaluru; Editing by Sonali Paul and Thomas Derpinghaus)

articles.body: Decommissioning November 10, 2026 · 2 hours ago Energean selects Swedish firm for post-decommissioning surveys in UK NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Njord Survey Swedish offshore survey company Njord Survey has won a contract with UK-based oil & gas player Energean for the provision of post-decommissioning site survey services at three fields in the UK Southern North Sea. We own our vessels and our survey equipment, and the people doing the work are full-time Njord Survey employees. That gives Energean one accountable team and a spread that is ours to schedule, from the first survey line to the final report. The UK is our largest market, and this contract is an important step for us in the North Sea decommissioning sector,” said Martin Wikmar , CEO of Njord Survey. Seanautics will support ONE’s customers through its offices in Damascus and Latakia, providing local access to the carrier’s international shipping network. The company has been active in the region for 25 years. Its local teams will assist customers with shipping enquiries and provide support for their transport and logistics needs. Expanding ONE’s regional network The new appointment builds on the established relationship between ONE and Seanautics in Lebanon. Through this arrangement, ONE aims to strengthen its customer services and develop its presence in the Syrian market. Tomohiro Hosaka, Managing Director of ONE Europe & Africa, said the expansion would help the carrier meet growing demand for shipping and logistics services in Syria. He also highlighted Seanautics’ local experience and knowledge of the market. Meanwhile, Raed G. Baconi, Deputy CEO of Seanautics Maritime Services LLC, welcomed the partnership. He said the company’s teams in Damascus and Latakia would support customers and help connect Syrian businesses with international markets. The agreement gives ONE a dedicated local representative in Syria. However, the carrier has not announced any new direct shipping services or port calls as part of the appointment. The new agency is expected to begin operations in January 2027, extending ONE’s commercial network across the Levant.

articles.body: ExxonMobil Takes First Step Toward Venezuela Oil Return Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 10, 2026 © Askar - stock.adobe.com / Adobe Stock ExxonMobil said on Monday it signed a memorandum of understanding with Venezuelan state oil company PDVSA to assess upstream oil opportunities, marking a potential return to the country nearly two decades after its assets were expropriated. The agreement is non-binding and does not commit Exxon to any specific project. "This memorandum is a meaningful first step, but any future investment would require stable policies, clear regulations, strong investment protections and competitive returns," Exxon said in a statement. The company did not say which projects or oil areas it was evaluating. A final joint-venture or production-sharing contract would be needed before Exxon could take part in exploration or production. If Exxon proceeds, it would mark a major return to Venezuela after former President Hugo Chavez's government expropriated its assets. It would also be a political win for US President Donald Trump, who has sought to remake Venezuela's oil sector with US companies in leading roles after American forces removed President Nicolas Maduro from power in January. At a signing ceremony broadcast by VTV, a state TV station, interim President Delcy Rodriguez welcomed Exxon back and said she hoped the memorandum would soon lead to concrete agreements. "We welcome you back," Rodriguez said, adding that Venezuela expected the partnership to bring benefits both to Exxon and to the Venezuelan people. She also said Exxon would invest under favorable conditions and within a framework of legal certainty to protect its operations. Before the expropriation, Exxon held a 41.67% stake in the Cerro Negro heavy crude project, now known as Petromonagas, as well as a 50% interest in the La Ceiba project in the southern Maracaibo basin. Exxon affiliates filed for arbitration against Venezuela at the World Bank's International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) in 2007. In 2014, ICSID awarded Exxon $1.6 billion plus interest. Venezuela has challenged the award and the dispute remains unresolved. Earlier this year, after oil reforms advanced by Rodriguez opened the sector to new entrants, Exxon CEO Darren Woods said progress had been made on fiscal and legal terms, but cautioned that the company was "not in a rush." articles.title: Odfjell Drilling firms up multi-year rig deal with Vår Energi
articles.summary: This secures firm work for the seven-year-old semi-submersible rig through 2031, with options extending to 2035.
articles.body: Contracts & Tenders November 10, 2026 · 3 hours ago Odfjell Drilling firms up multi-year rig deal with Vår Energi This secures firm work for the seven-year-old semi-submersible rig through 2031, with options extending to 2035. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 1 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Deepsea Bergen rig Source: Odfjell Drilling Scotland-headquartered offshore drilling contractor Odfjell Drilling has finalized a three-year contract with Norway’s Vår Energi for a 2019-built rig it purchased at the end of 2025, sealing a firm commitment that keeps the semi-submersible fully booked until early 2031. Following an initial letter of award (LOA) announced in September 2026, Odfjell Drilling has put pen to paper with Vår Energi, cementing a three-year deal that features additional options stretching all the way to 2035. As a result, the 2019-built Deepsea Bergen semi-submersible rig has lined up work on the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS) starting in early 2028, after it completes its existing contract. The firm scope of work for the new assignment covers three years. After the firm period ends, Vår Energi has four one-year-priced options for use of the drilling unit. This means the rig is fully booked until early 2031, with priced options which extend into early 2035. Odfjell Drilling acquired the semi-submersible rig from Northern Ocean in December 2025 and renamed it from Deepsea Bollsta to Deepsea Bergen. This contract comes shortly after Serica Energy hired an Odfjell Drilling-operated semi-submersible rig for a multi-well drilling campaign in the North Sea. articles.body: Operations Press Releases Splash Crew launches to put seafarers at the heart of maritime news Splash November 10, 2026 0 721 2 minutes read Splash Maritime Group has unveiled Splash Crew , its latest specialist news platform, with the ambition of becoming essential daily reading for seafarers, crewing professionals, shipmanagers, regulators and maritime technology companies worldwide. The new publication builds on Splash’s longstanding commitment to championing seafarers and examining the human side of an industry responsible for moving global trade. The platform delivers international news, interviews, analysis and features covering crew welfare, recruitment, retention, training, safety, working conditions, regulation, career development and the rapidly changing technologies being introduced onboard ships. The publication will also examine some of shipping’s most pressing workforce challenges, from seafarer shortages and fatigue to mental health, connectivity, criminalisation, abandonment and the implications of automation and the energy transition for those working at sea. Splash Crew is designed to bridge the gap between life onboard and decisions made ashore, bringing together perspectives from seafarers, fleet managers, crewing agencies, training institutions, technology providers and policymakers. “At Splash, we’ve always believed that seafarers deserve far more attention than they typically receive in the maritime media,” said Sam Chambers, co-founder and editorial director of Splash Maritime Group. “Shipping is very good at telling us that people are its greatest asset, but the reality onboard does not always match the rhetoric. We want Splash Crew to examine that gap, celebrate the people who make this extraordinary industry work and challenge practices that need to change. “Crucially, this isn’t just another crew welfare publication. We want to cover every aspect of working life at sea, from the technologies arriving on the bridge and in the engine room to the changing demands placed on today’s officers and ratings. Our ambition is to make Splash Crew the first site seafarers and shipmanagers turn to every day.” The launch follows Splash’s publication of its inaugural Seafarers Report in 2025, which examined the growing importance of bringing the voices of those working onboard into corporate decision-making. Splash Crew will apply the same editorial philosophy that has underpinned Splash’s growth over more than a decade: fast, independent, informed reporting that respects readers’ time. The new platform also provides a dedicated global audience for the companies developing solutions to improve shipboard operations, training, safety and quality of life at sea. Splash Crew joins an expanding portfolio of specialist maritime publications from the Singapore-headquartered media group, including SplashTech , Splash Ports , and Splash Cruise .
